speaker: Devi
title: Devi Recalls the Essence of the Rudrayāmala
sanskrit:
श्रुतं देि मया सिं रुद्रयामऱसम्भिम् ।
विकभेदमशेषेण सारात्सारविभागश् ॥ १ ॥
transliteration:
śrutaṃ devi mayā samyak rudrayāmala-sambhavam |
vika-bhedam aśeṣeṇa sārāt-sāra-vibhāgaśaḥ || 1 ||
translation: O Devi, I have heard well the teaching arising from the Rudrayāmala, with its divisions and distinctions in full, analyzed according to essence and the essence of essence.
intent_summary: The verse establishes that Devi has already received extensive scriptural teaching and is now seeking the deepest essential truth beyond doctrinal detail.
beginner_explanation: Devi begins by saying she has already heard many teachings and classifications from sacred texts. Even after learning all that, she still wants the deepest core. This sets up the text as a search for direct understanding, not just more information.
scholar_explanation: The opening situates the dialogue within the Tantric revelatory corpus, specifically the Rudrayāmala, while indicating that even exhaustive knowledge of bheda, vikalpa, and doctrinal stratification does not exhaust the highest truth. The phrase sārāt-sāra suggests a movement from layered śāstric exposition toward the innermost tattva. As in much of non-dual Śaiva scripture, scriptural multiplicity becomes the prelude to transcending conceptual differentiation.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Asks Bhairava's True Nature
sanskrit:
अद्यावऩ न वनिृत्तो मे सम्शय् ऩरमेश्वर ।
वकं रूऩं तत्त्वतो देि शब्दरावशकऱामयम् ॥ २ ॥
transliteration:
adyāpi na nivṛtto me saṃśayaḥ parameśvara |
kiṃ rūpaṃ tattvato deva śabda-rāśi-kalāmayam || 2 ||
translation: Even now, my doubt has not ceased, O Supreme Lord. What, in truth, is Your real form, O Deva? Is it constituted of the aggregate of sound and kalā (energetic phases/powers)?
intent_summary: The verse asks directly what Bhairava truly is in essence, beyond inherited formulations and symbolic descriptions.
beginner_explanation: Devi says that her doubt is still not resolved. She asks a simple but profound question: what is Bhairava really? She wonders whether the divine is made of sacred sound and subtle energies.
scholar_explanation: The question shifts from scriptural summary to ontological precision: tattvataḥ, 'in reality' or 'according to the truth.' Śabda-rāśi-kalāmaya evokes Tantric cosmology in which manifestation unfolds as sonic vibration, phonemic totality, and kalā-energies. Devi is probing whether Bhairava is to be identified with the articulated manifesting power or with something prior to and transcending it.

speaker: Devi
title: Is Bhairava Distinct from Shakti?
sanskrit:
वकं िा निात्मभेदेन भैरिे भैरिाकृतौ ।
विवशरोभेदवभन्नं िा वकं िा शविियात्मकम् ॥ ३ ॥
transliteration:
kiṃ vā navātma-bhedena bhairave bhairavākṛtau |
triśiro-bheda-bhinnaṃ vā kiṃ vā śakti-trayātmakam || 3 ||
translation: Or is Bhairava, in the form called Bhairava, divided as the ninefold self (navātman)? Or is He differentiated as the three-headed one? Or is He of the nature of the triad of powers (śakti-traya)?
intent_summary: The verse tests several established Tantric models to determine whether any of them adequately express Bhairava's true reality.
beginner_explanation: Devi continues by listing possible ways people describe the divine. Maybe Bhairava is a ninefold reality, or a threefold form, or a set of divine powers. She is asking whether these symbolic systems point to the final truth or only describe parts of it.
scholar_explanation: This verse invokes recognizable Śaiva-Tantric frameworks: navātman, triśiras/triadic differentiation, and śakti-traya, likely referring to icchā, jñāna, and kriyā-śakti. The questioning method is apophatic as much as doctrinal: Devi arrays authoritative categories only to expose their insufficiency as final definitions of anuttara. This anticipates Bhairava's deconstruction of representational theology in verses 9–10.

speaker: Devi
title: Is Bhairava Nada, Bindu, or Chakra?
sanskrit:
नादविन्दुमयं िावऩ वकं चन्द्राधधवनरोवधका् ।
चक्रारूढमनच्कं िा वकं िा शविस्वरूऩकम् ॥ ४ ॥
transliteration:
nāda-bindumayaṃ vāpi kiṃ candrārdha-nirodhikāḥ |
cakrārūḍham anackaṃ vā kiṃ vā śakti-svarūpakam || 4 ||
translation: Or is He made of nāda and bindu? Or of the crescent, nirodhikā, and the other subtle stages? Is He established in the chakra? Or beyond chakra? Or is He the very nature of Śakti?
intent_summary: The verse asks whether Bhairava is to be identified with subtle yogic structures and sonic stages, or with the underlying power behind them.
beginner_explanation: Devi now asks about inner yogic symbols: sacred sound, the point of origin, subtle phases, and energy centers. She is trying to find out whether the ultimate reality is one of these things, all of them, or something deeper. The question points toward direct experience rather than mere symbolism.
scholar_explanation: Nāda, bindu, candrārdha, and nirodhikā belong to subtle phonematic and yogic schemata associated with the ascent or involution of consciousness. The phrase cakrārūḍham anackam (textually uncertain but structurally clear) contrasts localization in esoteric supports with transcendence of structured supports. The interrogative movement presses toward the core Trika issue: is Bhairava reducible to stages of manifestation, or is He the non-objectifiable ground of Śakti itself?

speaker: Devi
title: How Can the Supreme Be Classified?
sanskrit:
ऩराऩराया् सकऱम् अऩरायाश्च िा ऩुन् ।
ऩराया यवद तद्वत्स्यात् ऩरत्वं तद् विरुध्यते ॥ ५ ॥
transliteration:
parāparāyāḥ sakalam aparāyāś ca vā punaḥ |
parāyā yadi tadvat syāt paratvaṃ tad virudhyate || 5 ||
translation: Is that whole reality of the para-aparā state, or again of the aparā state? If it were of the parā state in that way, then its very supremacy (paratva) would be contradicted.
intent_summary: The verse questions whether the Supreme can meaningfully be confined within standard hierarchical categories such as parā, parāparā, and aparā.
beginner_explanation: Devi is noticing a problem: if the highest reality is put into a category, does that make it less than truly absolute? She is challenging spiritual labels themselves. The point is that the deepest truth may not fit neatly into any system.
scholar_explanation: This verse engages the tripartite Śākta/Śaiva schema of parā, parāparā, and aparā, commonly used to map levels of manifestation and consciousness. Devi's logic is incisive: to classify the absolute as one stratum among others is already to limit it. The concern is fundamentally non-dual and anticipates Bhairava's refusal to identify his nature with any objectifiable ontological tier.

speaker: Devi
title: The Supreme Cannot Depend on Differentiation
sanskrit:
न वह िणधविभेदेन देहभेदेन िा भिेत् ।
ऩरत्वम् वनष्कऱत्वेन सकऱत्वे न तद्भिेत् ॥ ६ ॥
transliteration:
na hi varṇa-vibhedena deha-bhedena vā bhavet |
paratvaṃ niṣkalatvena sakalatve na tad bhavet || 6 ||
translation: For supremacy cannot arise through differentiation of letters/sounds (varṇa) or through differentiation of body/forms. Supremacy belongs to the partless (niṣkala); in that which is possessed of parts (sakala), it cannot be so.
intent_summary: The verse argues that the highest reality cannot be fully identified with differentiated sound-forms or embodied structures because the Supreme is fundamentally partless.
beginner_explanation: Devi says the ultimate cannot just be a collection of parts, forms, sounds, or bodies. If something is made of pieces, it is limited. So she points toward a reality that is whole and indivisible.
scholar_explanation: Varṇa may signify phonemes, mantric articulation, or differentiated expression; deha-bheda points to formed embodiments, including subtle and gross levels. By contrasting niṣkala and sakala, the verse invokes a classic Śaiva polarity: the unfragmented absolute versus manifest differentiated expression. Yet in Kashmir Śaivism, this distinction is often ultimately sublated, since the niṣkala is not elsewhere than the sakala but its non-dual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Praises the Question
sanskrit:
प्रसादं कुरु मे नाथ वन्शेषं विवि संशयम् ।
साधु साधु त्वया ऩृष्टं तन्त्रसारवमदं वप्रये ॥ ७ ॥
transliteration:
prasādaṃ kuru me nātha niḥśeṣaṃ chindhi saṃśayam |
sādhu sādhu tvayā pṛṣṭaṃ tantra-sāram idaṃ priye || 7 ||
translation: Grant me Your grace, O Lord; cut away my doubt completely. Well asked, well asked by you, O Beloved—this indeed is the very essence of Tantra.
intent_summary: The verse marks Devi's inquiry as exemplary and declares that the coming teaching reveals the core essence of Tantra.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava responds warmly and says her question is excellent. He confirms that this is not a side issue but the heart of the teaching. The text is telling us that sincere questioning is itself part of the path.
scholar_explanation: Although the transmitted lineation here reflects some textual compression, the sense is clear: Devi's saṃśaya becomes the doorway to upadeśa. Tantra-sāra here refers not to ritual complexity but to the distilled recognition of Bhairava's nature. The verse validates vicāra—penetrating inquiry—as integral to the non-dual revelation that follows.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Teaching Is Most Secret
sanskrit:
गूहनीयतमं भद्रे तथावऩ कथयावम ते ।
यविंवचत्सकऱम् रूऩम् भैरिस्य प्रकीवतधतम् ॥ ८ ॥
transliteration:
gūhanīyatamaṃ bhadre tathāpi kathayāmi te |
yat kiñcit sakalaṃ rūpaṃ bhairavasya prakīrtitam || 8 ||
translation: This is most deeply secret, O Auspicious One, yet I shall tell you: whatever formed or complete manifestation has been proclaimed as the form of Bhairava—
intent_summary: The verse introduces Bhairava's answer by stating that the teaching is highly esoteric and that conventional descriptions of Bhairava are about to be re-evaluated.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says this teaching is very secret, but he will reveal it anyway. He is about to explain that many usual descriptions of the divine are only partial. This prepares the listener to look beyond outer forms and ideas.
scholar_explanation: Gūhanīyatama underscores the initiatory character of the teaching, though its secrecy is existential rather than merely institutional. Sakala-rūpa here signals all describable, formed, or complete iconographic/doctrinal renderings of Bhairava. The trailing construction opens into a critical reassessment of representational theology in the next verse.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Conventional Forms Are Like Illusion
sanskrit:
तदसारतया देवि विऻेयं शक्रजाऱित् ।
मायास्वप्नोऩमं चैि गन्धिधनगरभ्रमम् ॥ ९ ॥
transliteration:
tad asāratayā devi vijñeyaṃ śakra-jālavat |
māyā-svapnopamaṃ caiva gandharva-nagara-bhramam || 9 ||
translation: That should be understood as lacking ultimate essence, O Devi—like Indra's net of illusion, like māyā, like a dream, like the bhrama of a gandharva-city in the sky.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that conceptual and symbolic forms of Bhairava are provisional appearances, not the ultimate essence itself.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava says that the forms and ideas people cling to are not the final truth. They are like dreams, mirages, or magical appearances. This does not mean they are useless, but they should not be mistaken for ultimate reality.
scholar_explanation: Asāratā does not imply total falsity in a crude sense, but lack of final substantiality when compared to svātantrya-consciousness. The stock images—śakra-jāla, svapna, māyā, gandharva-nagara—signal phenomenality as dependent appearance. In Pratyabhijñā terms, objective formulations of the divine are ābhāsas, valid as manifestations yet not exhaustive of Bhairava's anuttara nature.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Forms Are Given for the Deluded Mind
sanskrit:
ध्यानाथं भ्रान्तिुद्धीनाम् वक्रयाडम्बरिवतधनाम् ।
केिऱं िवणधतं ऩुंसां विकल्पवनहतात्मनाम् ॥ १० ॥
transliteration:
dhyānārthaṃ bhrānta-buddhīnām kriyā-ḍambara-vartinām |
kevalaṃ varṇitaṃ puṃsāṃ vikalpa-nihatātmanām || 10 ||
translation: These have been described merely for the sake of meditation for those whose minds are confused, who are occupied with the pomp of ritual action, and whose selves are struck down by conceptual constructions (vikalpa).
intent_summary: The verse teaches that symbolic forms and elaborate practices are provisional aids for minds still bound by conceptualization.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava explains that outer forms, rituals, and detailed images can help people who are not yet ready for direct experience. They are supports, not the destination. The real teaching will go beyond mental concepts and spiritual display.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic non-dual Śaiva demotion of externalized supports without rejecting their pedagogical function. Dhyānārtham indicates upāya: form-based contemplations are skillful means for those still entangled in kriyā-ḍambara and vikalpa. The implied trajectory is from conceptual support toward nirvikalpa recognition of Bhairava as immediate cit, a movement unfolded throughout the dhāraṇās of the text.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Beyond Sound and Form
sanskrit:
तत्त्वतो न निात्मासौ शब्दरावशनध भैरि् ।
न चासौ विवशरा देिो न च शविियात्मक् ॥ ११ ॥
transliteration:
tattvato na nijātmāsau śabdarāśi-śarīrakaḥ bhairi | 
na cāsau triśirā devo na ca śakti-trayātmakaḥ || 11 ||
translation: In truth, that essential Self is not a mass of sound, O Bhairavī; nor is that Deity the three-headed god, nor constituted of the three powers (śakti-traya).
intent_summary: This verse strips away symbolic and theological identifications so the practitioner does not mistake conceptual forms for Bhairava's true nature.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava is saying: do not confuse the ultimate reality with religious symbols, sounds, or imagined divine forms. These may help point the way, but they are not the final truth itself. The teaching begins by removing what the mind tends to cling to.
scholar_explanation: The verse negates iconic and mantric reductions of Bhairava: he is not merely śabda-rāśi, nor a mythic triśiras form, nor exhausted by the triadic śaktis. This is a classic apophatic move in Trika, where tattvataḥ the absolute exceeds both ritual-symbolic representation and cosmological schematization. The intent is to loosen upāsanā-bound cognition in preparation for direct recognition (pratyabhijñā).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Not Nada, Bindu, Moon, or Chakra Sequence
sanskrit:
नादविन्दुमयो िावऩ न चन्द्राधधवनरोवधका् ।
न चक्रक्रमसवम्भन्नो न च शविस्वरूऩक् ॥ १२ ॥
transliteration:
nāda-bindu-mayo vāpi na candra-ardha-nirodhikāḥ | 
na cakra-krama-sambhinno na ca śakti-svarūpakaḥ || 12 ||
translation: Nor is he made of nāda and bindu; nor of the crescent, half-moon, or other subtle stages; nor divided according to the sequence of the chakras; nor merely of the nature of śakti as an objectified formulation.
intent_summary: The verse warns that subtle yogic maps and esoteric structures are not themselves the ultimate nature of Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Even refined spiritual ideas—inner sound, points of light, moon-symbols, chakras, and energy models—are still not the final reality. They can be useful road signs, but Bhairava is not limited to any system. The teaching points beyond all spiritual diagrams.
scholar_explanation: Here Bhairava is further distinguished from tantric subtle-body schemata: nāda, bindu, candra-ardha, nirodhikā, and cakra-krama. The verse does not deny their soteriological utility; rather, it denies their ultimacy as tattva. In non-dual Śaivism, such structures belong to upāya, while Bhairava as anuttara transcends all sequentialized ontologies.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Provisional Teachings for the Unawakened
sanskrit:
अप्रिुद्धमतीनाम् वह एता िाऱविभीवषका् ।
मातृमोदकित्सिं प्रिृत्त्यथधमुदाहृतम् ॥ १३ ॥
transliteration:
aprabuddha-matīnām hi etā bāla-vibhīṣikāḥ | 
mātṛ-modaka-vat sarvaṃ pravṛtty-arthaṃ udāhṛtam || 13 ||
translation: For those of unawakened understanding, these are like childish frighteners; all this has been taught, like sweets given by a mother, for the sake of inducing engagement (pravṛtti).
intent_summary: This verse explains that symbolic doctrines and practices are compassionate teaching devices meant to guide immature understanding toward the path.
beginner_explanation: People need different kinds of help depending on where they are. So spiritual teachings sometimes use symbols, promises, warnings, or structured methods to attract attention and encourage practice. Bhairava says these are helpful beginnings, not the final destination.
scholar_explanation: The verse explicitly marks earlier symbolic formulations as pedagogical concessions for aprabuddha-matīnāṃ. The metaphors of bāla-vibhīṣikā and mātṛ-modaka indicate both deterrent and inducive strategies in tantric instruction. This aligns with the graded logic of upāyas: provisional constructs are not false in a crude sense, but strategically deployed for adhikāra-specific initiation into higher recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Inexpressible Supreme Reality
sanskrit:
वदक्काऱकऱनोन्मुिा देशोद्देशाविशेवषणी ।
व्यऩदेष्टुमशक्यासािकथ्या ऩरमाथधत् ॥ १४ ॥
transliteration:
dik-kāla-kalanonmuktā deśoddeśā-aviśeṣiṇī | 
vyapadeṣṭum aśakyāsāv akathyā paramārthataḥ || 14 ||
translation: Free from the divisions of direction, time, and measurement; undifferentiated by place or spatial designation—That cannot truly be indicated in speech; in the highest sense, it is inexpressible.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that ultimate reality cannot be captured by spatial, temporal, or linguistic categories.
beginner_explanation: The deepest truth is not somewhere else, not in a special time, and not confined to any location. Because language works by dividing things up, it cannot fully describe what has no boundaries. The point is to stop looking for the absolute as an object.
scholar_explanation: This is a concise statement of the transcendence of paramārtha over dik, kāla, kalana, and deśa-bheda. The inability of vyapadeśa to grasp it reflects the Trika view that anuttara is beyond conceptual delimitation (vikalpa) and linguistic objectification. Yet it is not sheer nothingness; rather, it is self-revealing and only 'akathya' from the standpoint of discursive designation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairavī as the Fullness of Inner Bliss
sanskrit:
अन्त् स्वानुभिानन्दा विकल्पोन्मुिगोचरा ।
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरिी भैरिात्मन् ॥ १५ ॥
transliteration:
antaḥ-svānubhava-ānandā vikalponmukta-gocarā | 
yāvasthā bharitākārā bhairavī bhairavātmanaḥ || 15 ||
translation: That state which is the bliss of inward self-experience, accessible only when free from conceptualization, and of the nature of complete fullness—that is Bhairavī, the very essence of Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse identifies the supreme state as inwardly realized, concept-free blissful fullness, revealing Bhairavī and Bhairava as non-separate.
beginner_explanation: The truth being described is not found by thinking more, but by directly tasting your own inner awareness. When mental chatter falls quiet, there is a sense of wholeness and aliveness already present. That fullness is called Bhairavī, inseparable from Bhairava.
scholar_explanation: Bhairavī is here defined as the avasthā of antaḥ-svānubhava-ānanda, available only beyond vikalpa and marked by bharitākāratā, plenary fullness. This is a strongly non-dual statement: śakti is not other than Bhairava, but his very ātman in dynamic self-revelation. The verse resonates with Trika accounts of vimarśa as the blissful self-apprehension of prakāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Stainless All-Pervading Reality
sanskrit:
तद्वऩुस्तत्त्वतो ऻेयं विमऱं विश्वऩूरणम् ।
एिं विधे ऩरे तत्त्वे क् ऩूज्य् कश्च तृप्यवत ॥ १६ ॥
transliteration:
tad vapuḥ tattvato jñeyaṃ vimalaṃ viśva-pūraṇam | 
evaṃ vidhe pare tattve kaḥ pūjyaḥ kaś ca tṛpyati || 16 ||
translation: That form, in truth, should be known as stainless and all-pervading, filling the whole universe. In such a supreme reality, who is to worship, and who indeed is to be satisfied?
intent_summary: This verse dissolves the duality of worshipper and worshipped by declaring the supreme reality to be universally present and non-separate.
beginner_explanation: If the divine fills everything completely, then there is no absolute separation between you and what you worship. The usual idea of one person offering devotion to something outside themselves begins to fall away. The verse invites a more direct, unified understanding of the sacred.
scholar_explanation: The verse moves from ontological fullness (viśva-pūraṇam) to liturgical non-duality: in the para-tattva, the polarity of pūjaka and pūjya collapses. This is a hallmark of the internalization of worship in Trika, where external ritual is ultimately subordinated to recognition of the all-pervasive, vimala nature of consciousness. The interrogative form serves to undercut residual dualistic religiosity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Supreme Goddess as Bhairava's State
sanskrit:
एिं विधा भैरिस्य यािस्था ऩवरगीयते ।
सा ऩरा ऩररूऩेण ऩरा देिी प्रकीवतधता ॥ १७ ॥
transliteration:
evaṃ vidhā bhairavasya yāvasthā parigīyate | 
sā parā para-rūpeṇa parā devī prakīrtitā || 17 ||
translation: Such is the state of Bhairava that is sung of; that, in its supreme form, is proclaimed to be the Supreme Goddess (Parā Devī).
intent_summary: The verse teaches that the supreme state of Bhairava is itself the Supreme Goddess, affirming the unity of consciousness and its power.
beginner_explanation: Bhairava and the Supreme Goddess are not two separate realities. The same ultimate state can be spoken of as pure divine consciousness or as the highest divine power. This helps us see that stillness and energy are one.
scholar_explanation: This verse identifies Bhairava's avasthā with Parā Devī, expressing a core Trika insight: śiva and śakti are distinguishable in discourse but non-different in essence. 'Para-rūpeṇa' signals not a secondary manifestation but the highest modality of reality itself. It prepares for the next verses' explicit articulation of śakti-śaktimat-abheda.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Inseparability of Power and Possessor
sanskrit:
शविशविमतोयधद्वद् अभेद् सिधदा वस्थत् ।
अतस्तद्धमधवमधत्वात् ऩराशवि् ऩरात्मन् ॥ १८ ॥
transliteration:
śakti-śaktimator yadvad abhedaḥ sarvadā sthitaḥ | 
atastad-dharma-dharmitvāt parā śaktiḥ parātmanaḥ || 18 ||
translation: Just as there is always no difference between power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat), so, by the relation of attribute and bearer of the attribute, the supreme Power belongs to the Supreme Self.
intent_summary: The verse clarifies that śakti and its source are never separate, establishing the non-duality of dynamic power and absolute consciousness.
beginner_explanation: A fire cannot be separated from its power to burn. In the same way, ultimate reality cannot be separated from its living energy or power. Bhairava and Śakti are two ways of talking about one reality.
scholar_explanation: The analogy formalizes śakti-śaktimat-abheda, central to Kashmir Śaiva metaphysics. Though phrased through dharma-dharmin language, the relation should not be read as strict substance-attribute dualism; rather, it points to an intrinsic non-difference between prakāśa and vimarśa, the luminous Self and its reflexive power. Parāśakti is thus the dynamic self-nature of parātman.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Like Fire and Its Burning Power
sanskrit:
न िह्नेदाधवहका शविव्यधवतवरिा विभाव्यते ।
केिऱम् ऻानसत्तायां प्रारम्भोऽयं प्रिेशने ॥ १९ ॥
transliteration:
na vahner dāhikā śaktir vyatiriktā vibhāvyate | 
kevalaṃ jñāna-sattāyāṃ prārambho 'yaṃ praveśane || 19 ||
translation: The burning power of fire is not conceived as separate from fire itself. This teaching is only a beginning, for entry into the reality of consciousness-being (jñāna-sattā).
intent_summary: The verse uses the fire analogy to introduce the practitioner into direct understanding that consciousness and its power are inseparable.
beginner_explanation: Just as you never find heat apart from fire, you do not find divine power apart from the divine itself. This explanation is given as a simple doorway into deeper understanding. It is meant to help the mind enter the teaching, not to trap it in theory.
scholar_explanation: The fire-heat analogy refines the prior claim of śakti-śaktimat-abheda in phenomenologically accessible terms. 'Jñāna-sattā' suggests the living reality of conscious being, and the verse explicitly self-identifies as merely a prārambha for praveśa—an initiatory conceptual bridge. Thus doctrine functions here as a preparatory upāya leading beyond discursivity into direct recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering Śakti, Becoming Śiva
sanskrit:
शक्त्यिस्थाप्रविष्टस्य वनविधभागेन भािना ।
तदासौ वशिरूऩी स्यात् शैिी मुखवमहोच्यते ॥ २० ॥
transliteration:
śakty-avasthā-praviṣṭasya nirvibhāgena bhāvanā | 
tadāsau śiva-rūpī syāt śaivī mukham ihocyate || 20 ||
translation: For one who has entered the state of Śakti, contemplation (bhāvanā) without division arises; then one becomes of the nature of Śiva. This is called here the Śaiva mouth, or gateway (mukha).
intent_summary: The verse teaches that by entering the undivided state of Śakti through nondual contemplation, the practitioner realizes identity with Śiva.
beginner_explanation: When you settle into the living energy of awareness without splitting experience into 'me' and 'that,' a deep shift happens. You begin to recognize the same divine nature within yourself. This verse presents that undivided entry as a doorway into realization.
scholar_explanation: Śakty-avasthā-praveśa culminates in nirvibhāga-bhāvanā, a non-differentiated contemplative assimilation in which the aspirant becomes śiva-rūpī. The expression 'śaivī mukham' implies a principal gateway into Śaiva realization: entry through śakti as the dynamic mode of the absolute. This accords with Trika's insistence that vimarśa is the practical portal to recognition of prakāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Śakti Reveals Śiva Like Light Reveals Forms
sanskrit:
यथाऱोकेन दीऩस्य वकरणैभाधस्करस्य च ।
ऻायते वदवविभागावद तद्वच्छक्त्या वशि् वप्रये ॥ २१ ॥
transliteration: yathā'lokena dīpasya kiraṇair bhāskarasya ca | jñāyate digvibhāgādi tadvac chaktyā śivaḥ priye || 21 ||
translation: Just as, by the light of a lamp or by the rays of the sun, the divisions of direction and other things are known, so too, O priya (Beloved), Śiva is known through Śakti.
intent_summary: This verse teaches that the transcendent reality of Śiva becomes knowable only through the manifesting power of Śakti.
beginner_explanation: A dark room is hard to understand until a lamp is lit. In the same way, pure reality is not grasped as an object by itself, but becomes evident through its living energy. The verse is saying that awareness and its power are not separate.
scholar_explanation: This is a concise theological statement of the inseparability of Śiva and Śakti, central to Trika and Pratyabhijñā thought. Śiva, as pure prakāśa (luminosity), is disclosed through Śakti as vimarśa, the self-revealing dynamism by which manifestation and recognition occur. The analogy of lamp-light and sun-rays emphasizes epistemic mediation without implying ontological duality.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Asks About the Formless State
sanskrit:
देिदेि विशूऱाङ्क कऩाऱकृतभूषण ।
वदवदेशकाऱशून्या च व्यऩदेशवििवजधता ॥ २२ ॥
transliteration: devadeva viśūlāṅka kapāla-kṛta-bhūṣaṇa | digdeśakālaśūnyā ca vyapadeśa-vivarjitā || 22 ||
translation: O God of gods, marked with trident-signs, adorned with a skull as ornament—she who is void of direction, place, and time, and free from all designation—
intent_summary: This verse introduces Devi’s inquiry into the indescribable, formless condition beyond spatial, temporal, and conceptual limitation.
beginner_explanation: Devi is speaking about a reality that cannot be pinned down. It is not somewhere, not at some time, and cannot really be named. She is asking how such a mysterious state can actually be known.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes iconic Bhairava imagery while immediately negating all limiting predicates: dik, deśa, kāla, and vyapadeśa. This movement from symbolic form to apophatic transcendence is characteristic of Tantric discourse, where deity-form serves as an entry into the anākhyā, the unsayable state beyond conceptual determination. The implied question concerns how the nirvikalpa reality of Bhairava is to be accessed.

speaker: Devi
title: Devi Requests the Means to the Supreme
sanskrit:
यािस्था भवरताकारा भैरिस्योऩऱभ्यते ।
कैरुऩायैमुधखम् तस्य ऩरा देवि कथं भिेत् ।
यथा सम्यगहम् िेवि तथा मे ब्रूवह भैरि ॥ २३ ॥
transliteration: yāvasthā bharitākārā bhairavasyopalabhyate | kair upāyair mukhaṃ tasya parā devi kathaṃ bhavet | yathā samyag ahaṃ vedaṁ tathā me brūhi bhairava || 23 ||
translation: That state in which the full (bharitākāra) nature of Bhairava is realized—by what means may one approach its entrance? How does the supreme, O Goddess, come to be? Tell me, Bhairava, in such a way that I may know it rightly.
intent_summary: Devi asks for direct practical means (upāya) to realize Bhairava’s all-pervasive fullness.
beginner_explanation: This is the turning point where philosophy becomes practice. Devi is not asking for more theory; she wants workable methods. She asks: how can someone actually enter this state and know it for themselves?
scholar_explanation: Verse 23 formally opens the upāya section of the text. The key phrase bharitākāra evokes Bhairava as plenitude, a fullness not opposed to emptiness but saturating all experience; the request for mukhaṃ tasya, the ‘entrance’ or ‘gateway,’ anticipates the 112 dhāraṇās as pragmatic portals into recognition (pratyabhijñā). The verse bridges ontological exposition and soteriological method.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Breath Junction Between Prāṇa and Jīva
sanskrit:
ऊर्ध्वे प्राणो ह्यधो जीिो विसगाधत्मा ऩरोच्चरेत् ।
उत्पवत्तवद्वतयस्थाने भरणाद्भवरता वस्थवत् ॥ २४ ॥
transliteration: ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret | utpatti-dvitaya-sthāne bharaṇād bhairavī sthitiḥ || 24 ||
translation: Prāṇa moves upward and jīva downward; the supreme emission-nature (visargātmā) arises forth. At the place where these two originate, by filling/attending there, there is the state of Bhairavī.
intent_summary: This verse teaches meditation on the junction-point of the upward and downward life-currents to enter the Bhairavī state.
beginner_explanation: Notice that the breath seems to move in two directions: up and down. Instead of following the whole movement, pay attention to the subtle meeting-point or source-point from which the movement begins. Resting awareness there opens a deeper stillness.
scholar_explanation: This foundational dhāraṇā works with the polarity of prāṇa and jīva/apāna, interpreted as ascending and descending currents within the subtle body. The term visarga points to the pulsation of emission, often linked with the haḥ- or outpouring principle of manifestation; by attending to the utpatti-dvitaya-sthāna, the source-junction of the two currents, one enters Bhairavī-sthiti, the dynamic non-dual state of awakened śakti-consciousness. It prefigures later kumbhaka and madhya-oriented contemplations.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bhairava Revealed in the Turning of the Breath
sanskrit:
मरुतोऽन्तिधवहिाधवऩ वियद्युवमावनितधनात् ।
भैरव्या भैरिस्येत्थं भैरवि व्यज्यते िऩु् ॥ २५ ॥
transliteration: maruto'ntar bahir vāpi viyad-yugmānivartanāt | bhairavyā bhairavasyetthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ || 25 ||
translation: When the breath (marut) turns back, whether inside or outside, through the pair of spaces, then in this way, O Bhairavī, the form of Bhairava is revealed through Bhairavī.
intent_summary: This verse instructs one to attend to the reversal point of the breath in inner and outer space, where Bhairava becomes manifest.
beginner_explanation: At the end of an inhale and the end of an exhale, the breath naturally turns. Those tiny turning points are very quiet and easy to miss. The verse says that if you notice them carefully, something profound is revealed there.
scholar_explanation: The key practice concerns the nivartana, the turning or reversal of marut at the inner and outer pauses, mapped onto the viyat-yugma, the ‘pair of spaces’ within and without. Bhairava is disclosed through Bhairavī—Śakti here functioning as the transitional vibrancy at the respiratory threshold. This is an early articulation of madhya-sādhana through spontaneous kumbhaka rather than forceful control.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abide in the Motionless Middle
sanskrit:
न व्रजेन्न विशेच्छविमधरुद्रूऩा विकावसते ।
वनविधकल्पतया मध्ये तया भैरिरूऩता ॥ २६ ॥
transliteration: na vrajen na viśec chaktir marudrūpā vikāsate | nirvikalpatayā madhye tayā bhairavarūpatā || 26 ||
translation: When the śakti, in the form of breath, neither goes out nor enters, then it expands. By means of that middle, in a state free of conceptualization (nirvikalpatayā), there is the condition of being Bhairava.
intent_summary: This verse points to the breathless middle state, free of mental construction, as a direct gateway to Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: There is a tiny moment when the breath is not going in and not going out. Usually the mind rushes past it. If you relax into that still middle without thinking about it, the verse says you touch a deeper level of awareness.
scholar_explanation: Here śakti is explicitly identified with marudrūpā, the breath-current itself, whose suspension reveals its expanded nature. The madhya is not merely a temporal pause but a non-conceptual opening in which vikalpa ceases; nirvikalpatā allows the practitioner to recognize bhairavarūpatā, the state of identity with Bhairava. This verse is doctrinally aligned with the central Trika emphasis on the middle as the locus of spanda and recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Peace at the End of Inhale, Exhale, and Retention
sanskrit:
कुवम्भता रेवचता िावऩ ऩूवरता िा यदा भिेत् ।
तदन्ते शान्तनामासौ शक्त्या शान्त् प्रकाशते ॥ २७ ॥
transliteration: kumbhitā recitā vāpi pūritā vā yadā bhavet | tadante śāntanāmāsau śaktyā śāntaḥ prakāśate || 27 ||
translation: Whether the breath is retained, exhaled, or inhaled—at the end of that, the one called Peace (śānta) is revealed; through Śakti, the peaceful one shines forth.
intent_summary: This verse teaches that the end-point of any phase of breath can disclose the peaceful luminous reality.
beginner_explanation: You do not need a complicated technique here. Simply notice the very end of breathing in, breathing out, or holding the breath. At that endpoint, there is a natural quietness that can reveal a deep inner peace.
scholar_explanation: The triad kumbhitā–recitā–pūritā encompasses retention, exhalation, and inhalation as equally valid entrances. Their anta, the terminal point of each phase, is the site where śānta—the quiescent aspect of ultimate reality—becomes manifest through śakti. The verse universalizes respiratory contemplations by privileging the liminal threshold rather than any one technical prāṇāyāma form.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplate the Subtle Ray Rising from the Root
sanskrit:
आमूऱाविरणाभासां सूक्ष्मात् सूक्ष्मतरावत्मकाम् ।
वचन्तयेत्ताम् वद्वषट्कान्ते श्याम्यन्तीम् भैरिोदय् ॥ २८ ॥
transliteration: āmūlā kiraṇābhāsāṃ sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatarātmikām | cintayet tāṃ dviṣaṭkānte śāmyantīṃ bhairavodayaḥ || 28 ||
translation: One should contemplate that radiance like a ray, arising from the root, whose nature is subtler than the subtle. As it comes to rest at the end of the twelve, there is the arising of Bhairava.
intent_summary: This verse instructs visualization of a subtle ascending current of light from the root to its point of quiescence, where Bhairava dawns.
beginner_explanation: Imagine a very fine thread of light rising upward from the base of the body. Follow it gently until it becomes quiet at its upper limit. That settling into stillness is the point of the meditation.
scholar_explanation: The imagery suggests kuṇḍalinī or a suṣumnā-based ascent from the mūla through a subtle luminous current (kiraṇābhāsā). The phrase dviṣaṭkānte likely indicates the terminal point of the twelvefold measure or locus, resonating with subtle-body schemata used in Kaula and Trika praxis. Bhairavodaya, the dawning of Bhairava, occurs not merely through ascent but through śāmyantīṃ—the cessation of movement in the terminal subtle point.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Lightning Ascent Through the Chakras
sanskrit:
उद्गच्छन्तं तवडद्रूऩाम् प्रवतचक्रं क्रमात्क्रमम् ।
ऊर्ध्वं मुवष्टियं याित् तािदन्ते महोदय् ॥ २९ ॥
transliteration: udgacchantaṃ taḍidrūpāṃ praticakraṃ kramāt kramam | ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭitrayaṃ yāvat tāvad ante mahodayaḥ || 29 ||
translation: One should perceive it rising upward like lightning, through each chakra, step by step; up to the measure of three fists above—there, at the end, is the great arising.
intent_summary: This verse teaches a stepwise inner ascent of a lightning-like current through the chakras to a transcendent culmination above.
beginner_explanation: Picture a flash of energy moving upward inside you, passing through one center after another. Let it rise beyond the head to a point slightly above. The verse says a great opening can happen there.
scholar_explanation: The taḍidrūpā image evokes the sudden, vibrant, and luminous character of awakened śakti. Praticakraṃ kramāt kramam points to sequential ascent through the psycho-energetic centers, culminating at a point ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭitrayaṃ—three fist-widths above, often correlated with dvādaśānta or a transcendent cranial locus. Mahodaya marks the expansive epiphany beyond the bounded somatic field.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transcending the Twelvefold Sequence
sanskrit:
क्रमद्वादशकं सम्यग् द्वादशाऺरभेवदतम् ।
स्थूऱसूक्ष्मऩरवस्थत्या मुक्त्वा मुक्त्वान्तत् वशि् ॥ ३० ॥
transliteration: krama-dvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣara-bheditam | sthūla-sūkṣma-para-sthityā muktvā muktvāntataḥ śivaḥ || 30 ||
translation: When the twelvefold sequence is properly pierced, divided as the twelve-syllabled measure, then by successively releasing the gross, the subtle, and the supreme states—having let go and let go—at the end there is Śiva.
intent_summary: This verse teaches progressive transcendence through a twelvefold subtle process by relinquishing all levels until only Śiva remains.
beginner_explanation: This method is about letting go layer by layer. First release the obvious physical level, then subtler inner experiences, then even the most refined spiritual sense of attainment. When nothing is clung to, what remains is the deepest reality.
scholar_explanation: The verse likely references a dvādaśaka schema—possibly breath-measure, mantra-sequence, chakra-range, or dvādaśānta-based subtle mapping—‘pierced’ through sustained contemplative penetration. The triad sthūla, sūkṣma, para suggests progressive transcendence of ontological and experiential strata; muktvā muktvā emphasizes iterative relinquishment rather than acquisition. Śiva here appears as the residuum after deconstructing all conditioned modalities, aligning the dhāraṇā with laya-oriented Trika praxis.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Arrow of Awareness Through the Brow Bridge
sanskrit:
तयाऩूयाधशु मूधाधन्तं भङ्क्त्वा भ्रूऺेऩसेतुना ।
वनविधकल्पं मन् कृत्वा सिोर्ध्वे सिधगोद्गम् ॥ ३१ ॥
transliteration:
tayā pūryāśu mūrdhāntaṃ bhittvā bhrūkṣepa-setunā |
nirvikalpaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā sarvordhve sarvagodgamam || 31 ||
translation: By that (power/breath), quickly filling up to the end of the head, and piercing through by the bridge of the eyebrows, making the mind free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), one attains the arising that is above all, pervading all.
intent_summary: Direct awareness upward through the brow-center into a thought-free state so that transcendent, all-pervading consciousness reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse suggests lifting your attention upward inside the head, especially toward the space between the eyebrows. The important part is not straining, but becoming quiet and free from mental chatter. When attention becomes steady and open, a larger sense of presence may appear.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to an ascent of śakti or prāṇa to the mūrdhānta, with passage through the bhrūkṣepa-setu, the subtle bridge at the brow center. The instruction culminates in nirvikalpa-manas, indicating suspension of vikalpa so that the sarvordhva, sarvagata reality of Bhairava may flash forth. This technique resonates with later Kaula and Trika mappings of the ājñā region as a threshold of transcendence.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the Five Voids
sanskrit:
वशवखऩऺैवश्चिरूऩैमधण्डऱै् शून्यऩञ्चकम् ।
ध्यायतोऽनुत्तरे शून्ये प्रिेशो हृदये भिेत् ॥ ३२ ॥
transliteration:
śikhī-pakṣaiś citra-rūpair maṇḍalaiḥ śūnya-pañcakam |
dhyāyato'nuttare śūnye praveśo hṛdaye bhavet || 32 ||
translation: Meditating on the fivefold void (śūnya-pañcaka) as variegated circular forms like peacock feathers, there arises entry into the unsurpassed Void (anuttara-śūnya) in the Heart.
intent_summary: Use contemplation of layered inner spaces or voids to enter the supreme, heart-centered Void beyond them all.
beginner_explanation: Here the practitioner imagines or senses several subtle inner spaces, almost like layered circles or luminous patterns. By staying with these spaces, attention is led into a deeper openness beyond all images. That deeper openness is said to open in the heart.
scholar_explanation: The śūnya-pañcaka may be read as five voids or spatial levels in the subtle body or cognition, here symbolized by citra-rūpa maṇḍalas resembling śikhī-pakṣa, peacock plumage. The practice is not fixation on imagery for its own sake, but a passage into anuttara-śūnya, the unsurpassed void identical with the hṛdaya of Bhairava-consciousness. This reflects the Trika use of śūnya as a graded contemplative device resolved in non-objective awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Any Thought Dissolved into the Void
sanskrit:
ईदृशेन क्रमेणैि यि कुिावऩ वचन्तना ।
शून्ये कुड्ये ऩरे ऩािे स्वयम् ऱीना िरप्रदा ॥ ३३ ॥
transliteration:
īdṛśena krameṇaiva yatra kutrāpi cintanā |
śūnye kuḍye pare pātre svayaṃ līnā varapradā || 33 ||
translation: By this very method, whatever thought may arise anywhere—into the void, a wall, or some external object—when it dissolves by itself, it bestows the boon.
intent_summary: Let any thought settle and dissolve into emptiness or an object of attention until spontaneous absorption occurs.
beginner_explanation: This verse says you do not need a special thought or perfect meditation object. Whatever appears in the mind can be allowed to fade into stillness. If you stop feeding it and simply watch it dissolve, that very moment can open into deep peace.
scholar_explanation: The phrase īdṛśena krameṇaiva extends the prior śūnya-oriented method into a general contemplative principle: any vṛtti may be traced to its own laya. The mention of śūnya, kuḍya, and pātra implies both internal void and external supports, indicating that the decisive factor is not the object but the self-dissolution (svayaṃ līnā) of cognition. Such spontaneous laya is varapradā because it reveals the non-substantiality of vikalpa and the background of Bhairava-awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Stillness at the Skull's End
sanskrit:
कऩाऱान्तमधनो न्यस्य वतष्ठन्मीवऱतऱोचन् ।
क्रमेण मनसो दार्ढ्ाधत् ऱऺयेत् ऱष्यमुत्तमम् ॥ ३४ ॥
transliteration:
kapālānta-mano nyasya tiṣṭhan mīlita-locanaḥ |
krameṇa manaso dārḍhyāt lakṣayet lakṣyam uttamam || 34 ||
translation: Placing the mind at the end of the skull, remaining with eyes closed, by the gradual steadiness of the mind one should perceive the supreme target.
intent_summary: Fix the mind at the crown or upper cranial limit and, through growing steadiness, recognize the highest reality.
beginner_explanation: Close the eyes and rest attention at the top or inner end of the head. Do not force anything; just stay there gently and steadily. Over time, the mind becomes firm and a subtler kind of awareness becomes noticeable.
scholar_explanation: Kapālānta here denotes the cranial limit, often interpreted as the upper inner locus where attention gathers near the brahmarandhra. The practice depends not on dramatic effort but on manaso dārḍhya, the stabilization of citta into one-pointedness until the lakṣya-uttama, the supreme aim, becomes evident. This verse sits at the intersection of subtle-body localization and nondual recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the Central Channel as Subtle Space
sanskrit:
मध्यनाडी मध्यसंस्था विससूिाभरूऩया ।
ध्यातान्तव्योमया देव्या तया देि् प्रकाशते ॥ ३५ ॥
transliteration:
madhya-nāḍī madhya-saṃsthā bisa-sūtrābha-rūpayā |
dhyātāntar-vyomayā devyā tayā devaḥ prakāśate || 35 ||
translation: Meditating on the central channel, situated in the middle, in the form of a lotus-fiber thread, as the inner space that is the Goddess, by that the Deva shines forth.
intent_summary: Contemplate the central channel as a subtle inner space-form of the Goddess until divine luminosity reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: Imagine a very fine, delicate line or channel running through the center of your being, like the thread inside a lotus stalk. It is not just a body image, but a way to sense a quiet inner space. Resting in that subtle middle can bring a feeling of clear inner light.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic suṣumnā-oriented dhāraṇā, though the text uses madhya-nāḍī and the image of bisa-sūtra, the filament of the lotus, to stress extreme subtlety. The nāḍī is not merely physiological but antar-vyoma and Devī herself—śakti as the central axis of manifestation and return. When this madhya is stably contemplated, devaḥ prakāśate: Bhairava appears as self-revealing consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sealing the Gates and Seeing the Point
sanskrit:
कररुद्धदृगस्त्रेण भ्रूभेदाद्द्वाररोधनात् ।
दृष्टे विन्दौ क्रमाल्लीने तन्मध्ये ऩरमा वस्थवत् ॥ ३६ ॥
transliteration:
kara-ruddha-dṛg-astreṇa bhrū-bhedād dvāra-rodhanāt |
dṛṣṭe bindau kramāl līne tan-madhye paramā sthitiḥ || 36 ||
translation: By blocking the sense-gates through the weapon of the eyes restrained by the hands, and by piercing the brow, when the point (bindu) is seen and gradually dissolved, in its center is the supreme state.
intent_summary: Close off sensory distraction, focus inward at the brow until the inner point appears and dissolves, revealing the supreme state within it.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to turning the senses inward, even physically helping that process by closing or reducing outer input. When attention becomes very concentrated, a tiny point of light or focus may appear inwardly. Staying with it until it softens or dissolves can open a very deep stillness.
scholar_explanation: The method evokes yonimudrā-like sensory sealing: kara-ruddha and dvāra-rodhana indicate blocking the external gateways to force inwardization (pratyāhāra). Bhrū-bheda and bindu-darśana then lead to the laya of the visual point, and the text states that paramā sthitiḥ is found in its center. This aligns bindu with the threshold where manifest cognition contracts into undivided awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Subtle Tilaka Point at Crown, Heart, and Dissolution
sanskrit:
धामान्त् ऺोभसम्भूतसूक्ष्माविवतऱकाकृवतम् ।
विन्दुं वशखान्ते हृदये ऱयान्ते ध्यायतो ऱय् ॥ ३७ ॥
transliteration:
dhāmānte kṣobha-sambhūta-sūkṣmāti-sūkṣma-tilakākṛtim |
binduṃ śikhānte hṛdaye layānte dhyāyato layaḥ || 37 ||
translation: Meditating on the bindu, a most subtle tilaka-like mark arising from inner vibration at the end of the radiance, at the top-knot, in the heart, or at the end-point of dissolution—there is absorption (laya).
intent_summary: Focus on the extremely subtle inner point appearing at key subtle loci until the mind dissolves into absorption.
beginner_explanation: The verse speaks of a tiny inner point, almost like a speck of light or a mark, noticed in very subtle places such as the crown or the heart. Rather than analyzing it, simply stay with it. Deep concentration on such a subtle point can make the mind sink into stillness.
scholar_explanation: The bindu is described as kṣobha-sambhūta, born of subtle inner pulsation or spanda, and as a sūkṣmāti-sūkṣma tilaka. Its contemplated loci—śikhānta, hṛdaya, and layānta—show the interchangeability of upper, central, and absorptive centers in Trika praxis. The fruit is laya, not as inert trance but as reabsorption into the source-vibration of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorption in the Unstruck Sound
sanskrit:
अनाहते ऩािकणेऽभिशब्दे सवरद्द्रुते ।
शब्दब्रह्मवण वनष्णात् ऩरं ब्रह्मावधगच्छवत ॥ ३८ ॥
transliteration:
anāhate pātra-karṇe'bhagna-śabde sarid-drute |
śabda-brahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati || 38 ||
translation: One who is immersed in the unstruck sound (anāhata), heard in the vessel of the ear, in the uninterrupted resonance flowing like a river—having become adept in Sound-Brahman, attains the Supreme Brahman.
intent_summary: Listen deeply to the continuous inner sound until it leads beyond sound itself to the supreme reality.
beginner_explanation: If you become very quiet, you may notice a subtle inner hum, ringing, or current of sound. This verse says to listen to that steady inner sound as if following a stream. By merging attention with it, awareness can open into something deeper than ordinary hearing.
scholar_explanation: This is a nāda-yoga dhāraṇā centered on anāhata-śabda, the unstruck inner sound perceived within the karṇa-pātra. The metaphor sarid-druta, flowing like a river, emphasizes continuity rather than discrete auditory events. Mastery of śabda-brahman becomes the doorway to para-brahman, echoing broader tantric and upaniṣadic trajectories from sonic manifestation to transcendental consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: AUM Dissolved into the Void
sanskrit:
प्रणिावदसमुच्चारात् प्लुतान्ते शून्यभािानात् ।
शून्यया ऩरया शक्त्या शून्यतामेवत भैरवि ॥ ३९ ॥
transliteration:
praṇavādi-samuccārāt plutānte śūnya-bhāvanāt |
śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi || 39 ||
translation: From the utterance of praṇava and similar sounds, at the end of the prolonged resonance, by contemplating the void, through the supreme power that is Void, one enters into voidness, O Bhairavī.
intent_summary: Chant a sacred sound, follow its fading resonance into silence, and merge into the void revealed there.
beginner_explanation: Make a long sound such as OM and listen carefully as it fades away. At the very end, there is a quiet gap or open stillness. Rest in that silence, because the verse says that this silence is not empty in a dead way, but full of living power.
scholar_explanation: Praṇava here functions as an upāya: vocalized sound is extended (pluta) until attention can track its vanishing edge. The crucial movement is from śabda to śūnya through śūnya-bhāvanā, culminating in union with parā śakti as voidness itself. In Trika terms, śūnyatā here is not nihilistic absence but the vibrant openness of anuttara.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Any Sound Entered at Beginning and End
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्यावऩ िणधस्य ऩूिाधन्तािनुभाियेत् ।
शून्यया शून्यभूतोऽसौ शून्याकार् ऩुमान्भिेत् ॥ ४० ॥
transliteration:
yasya kasyāpi varṇasya pūrvāntāv anubhāvayet | 
śūnyayā śūnya-bhūto'sau śūnyākāraḥ pumān bhavet || 40 ||
translation: One should experience the beginning and end of any sound whatsoever. By means of the void, becoming void-like, that person becomes of the form of the void.
intent_summary: Attend closely to the arising and fading of any sound until awareness becomes one with the silent void framing it.
beginner_explanation: Pick any sound—a bell, a word, a passing noise—and notice exactly when it begins and when it disappears. The verse points to the quiet space before and after the sound. By becoming familiar with that silent space, the mind itself starts to feel open and spacious.
scholar_explanation: Unlike the more specialized praṇava practice of the previous verse, this dhāraṇā universalizes the method to any varṇa or sonic event. The contemplative fulcrum lies in the pūrva and anta, the liminal thresholds where sound emerges from and resolves into śūnya. To become śūnya-bhūta and śūnyākāra is to recognize consciousness as the non-obstructed ground of all phonemic manifestation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorption in the End of Prolonged Sound
sanskrit:
तन्त्र्यावदिाद्यशब्देषु दीघेषु क्रमसवम्स्थते् ।
अनन्यचेता् प्रत्यन्ते ऩरव्योमिऩुभधिेत् ॥ ४१ ॥
transliteration:
tantry-ādi-vādya-śabdeṣu dīrgheṣu krama-saṃsthiteḥ |
ananya-cetāḥ pratyante para-vyomānu-bhavet || 41 ||
translation: In the long, continuous sounds of stringed and other musical instruments, unfolding in sequence, one whose attention is undivided should, at their ending, become aware of the supreme space (para-vyoma).
intent_summary: Use sustained external sound and especially its fading end-point as a doorway into the supreme inner space.
beginner_explanation: Listen closely to a long musical tone, like a string or bell, and follow it all the way until it disappears. Do not get distracted or think about the sound—just stay with it completely. At the very end, when the sound vanishes, notice the open stillness that remains.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā employs śabda as an upāya: the practitioner tracks a dīrgha nāda through its krama, then rests awareness at its pratyanta, the terminal edge. The instruction points beyond gross sound to para-vyoma, the supreme expanse identified with cidākāśa. It resonates with other VBT techniques using sonic cessation as a trigger for recognition (pratyabhijñā) of Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mantric Ascent through Bindu and Nāda into the Void
sanskrit:
वऩण्डमन्त्रस्य सिधस्य स्थूऱिणधक्रमेण तु ।
अधेन्दुविन्दुनादान्त् शून्योच्चाराद्भिेवच्छि् ॥ ४२ ॥
transliteration:
piṇḍa-mantrasya sarvasya sthūla-varṇa-krameṇa tu |
ardhendu-bindu-nādāntāḥ śūnyoccārād bhavec chivaḥ || 42 ||
translation: For any embodied mantra, by proceeding through the sequence of its gross phonemes, and then through half-moon, bindu, and the end of nāda, through the utterance into the void (śūnyoccāra), one becomes Śiva.
intent_summary: Trace mantra from gross audible sound into subtler and subtler phases until it dissolves in the void beyond sound.
beginner_explanation: A mantra can be followed like a sound that becomes finer and finer. First there are the spoken syllables, then subtler inner aspects, until even sound itself fades into silence. Resting in that silent source is the heart of the practice.
scholar_explanation: The verse outlines the classic tantric gradation from sthūla-varṇa to subtle mantra-elements: ardhendu, bindu, and nādānta. Śūnyoccāra here suggests not mere absence but the transcendence of articulated phonation into the unstruck matrix of consciousness. The culmination, bhavec chivaḥ, indicates identity with Śiva through the reabsorption (laya) of vāc into its source.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Simultaneous Contemplation of the Body as Space
sanskrit:
वनजदेहे सिधवदक्कम् युगऩद्भाियेवद्वयत् ।
वनविधकल्पमनास्तस्य वियत्सिधम् प्रितधते ॥ ४३ ॥
transliteration:
nija-dehe sarva-dikkam yugapad bhāvayed viyat |
nirvikalpa-manās tasya viyat sarvaṃ pravartate || 43 ||
translation: Within one's own body, one should simultaneously contemplate space (viyat) in all directions. For one whose mind becomes free of conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), all appears as space.
intent_summary: Perceive the body not as a solid object but as open space in every direction until conceptual fixation relaxes.
beginner_explanation: Instead of feeling your body as dense and closed, imagine it as open and spacious everywhere at once. Front, back, above, below, inside—let it all feel airy and unobstructed. As this deepens, the usual sense of mental tightness can soften into openness.
scholar_explanation: The body is used here as a support for the expansion of viyat-bhāvanā, dissolving the habitual boundedness of embodiment. Yugapat is significant: spatiality is not sequentially imagined but intuited simultaneously, leading toward nirvikalpa-citta. The result is an ontological shift in which phenomena are apprehended as pervaded by ākāśa, recalling the non-obstruction of consciousness itself.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Void at Back and Root
sanskrit:
ऩृष्टशून्यम् मूऱशून्यम् युगऩद्भाियेच्च य् ।
शरीरवनरऩेवऺण्या शक्त्या शून्यमना भिेत् ॥ ४४ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭha-śūnyaṃ mūla-śūnyaṃ yugapad bhāvayec ca yaḥ | 
śarīra-nirapekṣiṇyā śaktyā śūnya-manā bhavet || 44 ||
translation: Whoever contemplates the void behind and the void at the root simultaneously, by a power (śakti) independent of bodily reference, becomes one whose mind is void-like.
intent_summary: Contemplate emptiness at key bodily poles until awareness becomes independent of bodily fixation and takes on the character of voidness.
beginner_explanation: Feel the open space behind you and at the base of the body at the same time. Rather than focusing on the body as a thing, let attention sense the emptiness around and through it. This can loosen the feeling of being trapped inside a solid form.
scholar_explanation: Pṛṣṭha-śūnya and mūla-śūnya function as polar loci for destabilizing corporeal identity. The phrase śarīra-nirapekṣiṇyā śaktyā suggests an activation of awareness not dependent on ordinary somatic reference, a śakti that discloses śūnya as intrinsic to embodiment. The culmination, śūnya-manā bhavet, is not nihilism but the mind's release into non-objective spaciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Threefold Void in Back, Root, and Heart
sanskrit:
ऩृष्टशून्यं मूऱशून्यं हृच्छून्यं भाियेविरम् ।
युगऩवन्नविधकल्पत्वावन्नविधकल्पोदयस्तत् ॥ ४५ ॥
transliteration:
pṛṣṭha-śūnyaṃ mūla-śūnyaṃ hṛc-chūnyaṃ bhāvayen niram |
yugapannirvikalpatvān nirvikalpodayas tataḥ || 45 ||
translation: One should steadily contemplate the void behind, the void at the root, and the void in the heart. Because of simultaneous non-conceptuality, from that there arises the state of nirvikalpa.
intent_summary: Hold multiple inner void-points at once so that the mind cannot maintain ordinary conceptual structuring.
beginner_explanation: Sense emptiness behind you, at the base of the body, and in the heart area all at once. This is harder for the thinking mind to manage, so it can briefly stop its usual chatter. In that pause, a more direct and open awareness may appear.
scholar_explanation: By multiplying loci of śūnya-bhāvanā—pṛṣṭha, mūla, and hṛd—the verse strategically overloads discursive mentation. Yugapad contemplation induces nirvikalpatva, not merely as absence of thought but as a shift to non-dual immediacy. The heart-space (hṛc-chūnya) also subtly links this practice to hṛdaya-centered Śaiva contemplations of consciousness as interior vastness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Momentary Perception of Void in Any Bodily Region
sanskrit:
तनूदेशे शून्यतैि ऺणमािं विभाियेत् ।
वनविधकल्पं वनविधकल्पो वनविधकल्पस्वरूऩभाक् ॥ ४६ ॥
transliteration:
tanū-deśe śūnyataiva kṣaṇa-mātraṃ vibhāvayet |
nirvikalpaṃ nirvikalpo nirvikalpa-svarūpa-bhāk || 46 ||
translation: In any region of the body, one should perceive only voidness for even a single moment. Becoming free of conceptualization, one comes to partake of the very nature of nirvikalpa.
intent_summary: Briefly perceive any part of the body as empty rather than solid, and use that instant to enter non-conceptual awareness.
beginner_explanation: Pick any part of the body—hand, chest, head—and for just a moment feel it as open emptiness instead of matter. Even a short glimpse can interrupt the habit of taking the body as fixed and solid. That crack in the usual view is the meditation.
scholar_explanation: This verse radicalizes śūnya-bhāvanā through minimal temporal demand: kṣaṇa-mātram suffices. The body-part (tanū-deśa) serves as a localized gateway through which conceptual embodiment is suspended, revealing nirvikalpa-svarūpa. The repetition of nirvikalpa underscores transformation of both mental mode and ontological identity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing All Bodily Substance as Pervaded by Space
sanskrit:
सिं देहगतं द्रव्यं वियद्व्याप्तं मृगेऺणे ।
विभाियेत्ततस्तस्य भािना सा वस्थरा भिेत् ॥ ४७ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ deha-gataṃ dravyaṃ viyad-vyāptaṃ mṛgekṣaṇe |
vibhāvayet tatas tasya bhāvanā sā sthirā bhavet || 47 ||
translation: O doe-eyed one, one should contemplate all the substance contained in the body as pervaded by space. Then that contemplation of his becomes steady.
intent_summary: Stabilize meditation by recognizing the entire body and its contents as thoroughly permeated by space.
beginner_explanation: Feel that everything in the body—flesh, bones, organs, breath—is filled with space. Not just surrounded by space, but gently opened by it from within. This helps the meditation become more natural and stable.
scholar_explanation: The verse extends viyat-bhāvanā from selected loci to sarvaṃ deha-gataṃ dravyaṃ, the whole material aggregate of embodiment. Viyad-vyāpta indicates interpenetration rather than mere external surrounding, softening substantialist assumptions about the body. Sthiratā of bhāvanā suggests that stable contemplative absorption emerges once spatial non-obstruction is universally intuited.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the Body's Inner Unseparated Space
sanskrit:
देहान्तरे त्ववविभागम् वभवत्तभूतम् विवचन्तयेत् ।
न वकंवचदन्तरे तस्य ध्यायन्नध्येयभाग्भिेत् ॥ ४८ ॥
transliteration:
dehāntare tv avibhāgaṃ bhitti-bhūtaṃ vicintayet |
na kiṃcid antare tasya dhyāyann adhyeya-bhāg bhavet || 48 ||
translation: One should contemplate, within the body, an undivided expanse serving as its supporting ground. Meditating that there is nothing at all inside it, one becomes of the nature of the meditated object.
intent_summary: Perceive the body's interior as an undivided empty field and merge with that very object of meditation.
beginner_explanation: Imagine the inside of the body as one continuous open field, not a collection of separate parts. Then feel that there is actually nothing solid there to hold onto. As you keep resting in that, you begin to take on the quiet quality of what you are meditating on.
scholar_explanation: Avibhāga, non-division, is central here: the body's interior is reimagined as a unitary field rather than a differentiated aggregate. Bhitti-bhūtaṃ may be read as the foundational support, suggesting the subtle 'ground' of embodiment is spacious consciousness rather than material structure. The phrase adhyeya-bhāg bhavet implies contemplative assimilation, where meditator and meditated lose their distinction.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting in the Sky of the Heart
sanskrit:
हृद्याकाशे वनऱीनाऺ् ऩिसम्पुटमध्यग् ।
अनन्यचेता् सुभगे ऩरं सौभावयमाप्नुयात् ॥ ४९ ॥
transliteration:
hṛdy ākāśe nilīnākṣaḥ padma-sampuṭa-madhyagaḥ |
ananya-cetāḥ subhage paraṃ saubhāgyam āpnuyāt || 49 ||
translation: With the eyes withdrawn and absorbed in the space of the heart, abiding in the center of the lotus-cup, with undivided awareness, O fortunate one, one attains supreme blessedness.
intent_summary: Withdraw attention inward into the heart-space and rest steadily in its subtle center.
beginner_explanation: Let the eyes become quiet, as if they are turning inward rather than looking out. Then rest attention in the center of the chest, imagined as a subtle open lotus or inner chamber. Staying there gently and fully can bring a deep feeling of grace and inner fullness.
scholar_explanation: Hṛd-ākāśa is a key Śaiva contemplative locus, the interiorized expanse where consciousness recognizes itself. Nilīnākṣaḥ implies sensory withdrawal without force, while padma-sampuṭa-madhyagaḥ evokes the subtle heart-lotus as both enclosure and opening. Paraṃ saubhāgyam here may be read as supreme blessedness, but also as the attainment of the supreme fortune of Śiva-recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mind-Dissolution at the Dvādaśānta
sanskrit:
सिधत् स्वशरीरस्य द्वादशान्ते मनोऱयात् ।
दृढिुद्धेदृधढीभूतं तत्त्वऱक्ष्यं प्रितधते ॥ ५० ॥
transliteration:
sarvataḥ sva-śarīrasya dvādaśānte mano-layāt |
dṛḍha-buddher dṛḍhī-bhūtaṃ tattva-lakṣyaṃ pravartate || 50 ||
translation: Through the dissolution of mind at the dvādaśānta, extending from all sides of one's own body, for one of firm understanding there arises the firmly established lakṣya of Reality (tattva-lakṣya).
intent_summary: Let the mind dissolve in the subtle terminal point beyond the body until reality reveals itself with certainty.
beginner_explanation: Sense a subtle point of openness just beyond the body's usual limits—the traditional teaching places this at the 'twelve-finger' endpoint. Let the mind rest and fade there instead of staying crowded inside thoughts. With steady practice, this can bring a clear and stable sense of what is most real.
scholar_explanation: Dvādaśānta, the terminal point twelve aṅgulas beyond, is a crucial locus in Śaiva yoga for prāṇa- and manas-laya. Here it is contemplated not merely above but 'from all sides' of the body, suggesting a total extension and de-centering of embodied identity. Tattva-lakṣya denotes the direct target or mark of reality, firmly manifest for one whose buddhi is stabilized in non-dual recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Awareness at the Dvādaśānta
sanskrit:
यथा तथा यि ति द्वादशान्ते मन् वऺऩेत् ॥
प्रवतऺणम् ऺीणिृत्तेिैऱऺण्यं वदनैभधिेत् ॥ ५१ ॥
transliteration:
yathā tathā yatra tatra dvādaśānte manaḥ kṣipet |
pratikṣaṇaṃ kṣīṇa-vṛtter vailakṣaṇyaṃ vidadhāti || 51 ||
translation: Wherever and however one may be, one should cast the mind into the dvādaśānta (the point twelve finger-breadths beyond the ordinary center). At every moment, as mental modifications (vṛttis) diminish, a distinctive state of otherness/exceptionality reveals itself.
intent_summary: Direct the mind into the dvādaśānta so that the fading of thought-waves discloses an extraordinary state of awareness.
beginner_explanation: This verse says to place attention in a subtle point just beyond the usual sense of yourself. By repeatedly resting attention there, ordinary thoughts begin to thin out. When that happens, a different kind of clear, spacious awareness starts to show itself.
scholar_explanation: The dvādaśānta is a key subtle locus in Śaiva and Tantric praxis, often correlated with the terminal point of prāṇa, mantra, or awareness. The instruction is less anatomical than phenomenological: manaḥ-kṣepa into this liminal point attenuates vṛtti and reveals vailakṣaṇya, the distinctive non-ordinary mode of consciousness. This resonates with VBT practices centered on spatial thresholds and the emergence of Bhairava through interruption of discursivity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating One's City Burned by Time-Fire
sanskrit:
काऱाविना काऱऩदादुवत्थतेन स्वकं ऩुरम् ।
प्लुष्टं विवचन्तयेदन्ते शान्ताभासस्तदा भिेत् ॥ ५२ ॥
transliteration:
kālāgninā kāla-padād utthitena svakaṃ puram |
pluṣṭaṃ vicintayed ante śāntābhāsas tadā bhavet || 52 ||
translation: One should contemplate one's own city (body, embodied domain) as scorched by the fire of Time, arising from the region/footing of Time. In the end, then, there arises the appearance of peace (śānta-ābhāsa).
intent_summary: Visualize the embodied self and its world as consumed by the fire of Time so that profound peace emerges beyond attachment.
beginner_explanation: Imagine that everything you normally cling to—your body, your life-structure, your personal world—is being burned away by time itself. This is not meant to frighten you, but to loosen your grip on what never lasts. When you deeply accept impermanence, a quiet peace can appear.
scholar_explanation: Kālāgni, the fire of Time, is a classic image of cosmic dissolution and the devouring power of Bhairava. Svakaṃ puram may indicate the psychophysical organism or the individual 'city' of embodiment; its incineration is a contemplative laya enacted through memento mori. The resulting śāntābhāsa is the peaceful luminosity that remains when temporal identification is consumed.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the Whole World as Dissolving
sanskrit:
एिम् एि जगत्सिं दवधं ध्यात्वा विकल्पत् ।
अनन्यचेतस् ऩुम्स् ऩुम्भाि् ऩरमो भिेत् ॥ ५३ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva jagat sarvaṃ dagdhaṃ dhyātvā vikalpataḥ |
ananya-cetasā puṃsaḥ puṃbhāvaḥ paramo bhavet || 53 ||
translation: In just this way, having meditated that the entire universe is burned up and dissolved from conceptual construction (vikalpa), for a person of undivided mind (ananya-cetas), the supreme state of Personhood/Being (puṃbhāva) arises.
intent_summary: By meditating on the whole universe as dissolved beyond conceptual thought, the practitioner realizes the supreme state of essential being.
beginner_explanation: Now the practice becomes bigger: not just your personal world, but the whole universe is imagined as dissolved. When the mind stops dividing and naming everything, a deeper sense of pure presence can appear. The verse points to what remains when mental storytelling falls away.
scholar_explanation: The phrase vikalpataḥ suggests the burning away not merely of objects but of the conceptualizing structure that sustains phenomenal multiplicity. Ananya-cetas indicates non-dispersed awareness, while puṃbhāvaḥ paramaḥ may be read as the supreme Self-state, the full emergence of Bhairava-consciousness beyond contracted individuality. This verse extends the prior kālāgni visualization into cosmological nondual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the Tattvas Within Body and World
sanskrit:
स्वदेहे जगतो िावऩ सूक्ष्मसूक्ष्मतरावण च ।
तत्त्वावन यावन वनऱयं ध्यात्वान्ते व्यज्यते ऩरा ॥ ५४ ॥
transliteration:
svadehe jagato vāpi sūkṣma-sūkṣmatarāṇi ca |
tattvāni yāni nilayaṃ dhyātvānte vyajyate parā || 54 ||
translation: Whether in one's own body or in the universe, meditating on the principles (tattvas)—subtle and still subtler—and on their ground/source (nilaya), at the end the Supreme (parā) becomes manifest.
intent_summary: Contemplate the subtle principles composing body and cosmos, together with their source, until the Supreme reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: This verse says your body and the universe are built from the same layers or principles. If you carefully contemplate these from the gross to the very subtle, and trace them back to their source, the deepest reality becomes visible. It is a way of seeing that inner and outer are not separate.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes the tattva-schema foundational to Trika and broader Śaiva cosmology, but its aim is not scholastic enumeration alone. By tracing the sūkṣma and sūkṣmatara tattvas in deha and jagat back to their nilaya, the practitioner realizes parā, the transcendent-yet-immanent supreme consciousness. This is a contemplative collapse of microcosm and macrocosm into their nondual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Heart Through the Subtle Current
sanskrit:
ऩीनां च दुिधऱां शविं ध्यात्वा द्वादशगोचरे ।
प्रविश्य हृदये ध्यायन्मुि् स्वातन्त्र्यमाप्नुयात् ॥ ५५ ॥
transliteration:
pīnām ca durbalāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśa-gocare |
praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktaḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt || 55 ||
translation: Meditating on the śakti, whether full/strong or weak/subtle, within the field of the twelve (dvādaśa-gocara), and entering into the heart, one who meditates thus becomes liberated and attains freedom (svātantrya).
intent_summary: Attend to the subtle power moving in the dvādaśānta field and let it enter the heart, where liberation and inner freedom are realized.
beginner_explanation: This verse asks you to notice subtle energy, whether it feels strong or very faint. Follow it inward into the heart—not just the physical organ, but the deep inner center of being. Resting there brings a sense of release and natural freedom.
scholar_explanation: Though the text is somewhat unstable, śakti here appears as a subtle current apprehended in the dvādaśa-gocara, likely linked with prāṇic extension or the field of awareness beyond the body. The movement into hṛdaya recalls the centrality of the Heart in nondual Śaiva realization as the locus of aham and spanda. Svātantrya, a cardinal Śaiva concept, denotes not mere psychological freedom but the innate autonomy of Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Sequential Contemplation of the Cosmic Pathways
sanskrit:
भुिनार्ध्वावदरूऩेण वचन्तयेत्क्रमशोऽवखऱम् ।
स्थूऱसूक्ष्मऩरवस्थत्या यािदन्ते मनोऱय् ॥ ५६ ॥
transliteration:
bhuvanādhvādi-rūpeṇa cintayet kramaśo 'khilam |
sthūla-sūkṣma-para-sthatyā yāvad ante mano-layaḥ || 56 ||
translation: One should contemplate the whole, in sequence, as consisting of the bhuvana-adhvan and the other pathways/levels. Through the stages of gross, subtle, and supreme abiding, there is finally dissolution of the mind (mano-laya).
intent_summary: Contemplate the full graded structure of reality from gross to supreme until the mind dissolves into its source.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses a step-by-step way of looking at reality. You start with obvious, outer things, then move to subtler levels, and finally toward the highest, most formless level. As attention follows this inward progression, the ordinary mind naturally quiets and dissolves.
scholar_explanation: The reference to adhvan evokes the sixfold pathways of manifestation recognized in Śaiva Tantra—such as bhuvana, tattva, mantra, and related ontological series. Kramaśaḥ contemplation from sthūla to sūkṣma to para is not mere cosmography but an interiorized ascent ending in mano-laya. The verse exemplifies how tantric metaphysics becomes a meditative ladder whose completion is absorption in Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on Śaiva Reality Through the Adhvan Process
sanskrit:
अस्य सिधस्य विश्वस्य ऩयधन्तेषु समन्तत् ।
अर्ध्वप्रवक्रयया तत्त्वं शैिं ध्यत्वा महोदय् ॥ ५७ ॥
transliteration:
asya sarvasya viśvasya paryanteṣu samantataḥ |
adhva-prakriyayā tattvaṃ śaivaṃ dhyātvā mahodayaḥ || 57 ||
translation: At the limits and extensions of this entire universe, on every side, by means of the adhvan-process one should meditate on the Śaiva reality (śaiva-tattva); then a great arising/dawn (mahodaya) occurs.
intent_summary: Use the cosmological pathways of manifestation to contemplate Śaiva reality throughout the whole universe, leading to a great awakening.
beginner_explanation: Here the instruction is to see the whole universe as expressing one sacred reality. By tracing everything back through its levels and connections, you begin to sense a great opening or awakening. The point is not to get lost in complexity, but to see one truth shining through all forms.
scholar_explanation: Adhva-prakriyā indicates contemplative use of the ordered pathways of manifestation rather than abstract ontology alone. Śaiva-tattva here is the all-pervading reality of Bhairava recognized at the 'edges' and totality of viśva, yielding mahodaya—a great upsurge of recognition (pratyabhijñā-like awakening). This verse stands at the junction of cosmological mapping and nondual realization.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the Universe as Void
sanskrit:
विश्वमेतन्महादेवि शून्यभूतं विवचन्तयेत् ।
तिैि च मनो ऱीनं ततस्तल्लयभाजनम् ॥ ५८ ॥
transliteration:
viśvam etan mahādevi śūnya-bhūtaṃ vicintayet |
tatraiva ca mano līnaṃ tatas tal-laya-bhājanam || 58 ||
translation: O Great Goddess, one should contemplate this entire universe as become void (śūnya). There itself the mind is dissolved; then one becomes a vessel of that dissolution.
intent_summary: Contemplate the entire universe as void so that the mind dissolves into that very emptiness.
beginner_explanation: Imagine that everything you see and know is made of openness rather than solid separateness. If you keep resting in that sense of vast emptiness, the mind stops gripping things so tightly. Then you begin to merge with that openness instead of standing apart from it.
scholar_explanation: Śūnya here is not mere negation but a contemplative gateway into the ungraspable ground beyond objectification. The instruction culminates in mano-laya within the very field contemplated, making the practitioner tal-laya-bhājana, one fit for or possessed by that absorption. The verse aligns with nondual Śaiva usages of void as a threshold to Bhairava rather than a final nihilistic conclusion.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fixing Vision on the Support Behind the Vessel
sanskrit:
घटावदभाजने दृवष्टं वभवत्तस्त्यक्त्वा विवनवऺऩेत् ।
तल्लयं तत्क्षणाद्गत्वा तल्लयात्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ५९ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādi-bhājane dṛṣṭiṃ bhittis tyaktvā vinikṣipet |
tal-layaṃ tat-kṣaṇād gatvā tal-layāt tanmayo bhavet || 59 ||
translation: In observing a vessel such as a pot, one should cast the gaze, abandoning the wall/supporting appearance, into that (deeper field). Attaining absorption in that at that very moment, and through that absorption, one becomes one with it.
intent_summary: Look past the object’s surface support into the underlying field until immediate absorption and identification occur.
beginner_explanation: Instead of looking at an object in the usual way, let your attention slip beyond its obvious form. Look through the thing, not just at it. If attention relaxes deeply enough, the separation between you and what is seen can suddenly dissolve.
scholar_explanation: The verse exploits perceptual deconstruction: the object (ghaṭa, etc.) is not taken as a solid independent entity but as a doorway to its supporting ground. By releasing fixation on delimiting form (here suggested by bhitti or surface/support), dṛṣṭi enters the subtler field, producing instantaneous laya and tanmayatā. Such practice reflects the Pratyabhijñā insight that objecthood veils the underlying continuum of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fixing the Gaze on Vast Featureless Space
sanskrit:
वनिृधऺवगवरवभत्त्यावददेशे दृवष्टं विवनवऺऩेत् ।
विऱीने मानसे भािे िृवत्तऺीण् प्रजायते ॥ ६० ॥
transliteration:
nirvṛkṣa-giri-bhitty-ādi-deśe dṛṣṭiṃ vinikṣipet |
vilīne mānase bhāve vṛtti-kṣīṇā prajāyate || 60 ||
translation: One should cast the gaze into a place devoid of trees, mountains, walls, and the like. When the mental state dissolves, there arises the exhaustion of mental modifications (vṛtti-kṣaya).
intent_summary: Rest the gaze in an unobstructed expanse so that mental activity dissolves and thought-waves fade away.
beginner_explanation: Find an open, empty view with as few visual distractions as possible. Rest your gaze there without chasing thoughts. The openness outside helps create openness inside, and the mind’s usual movements begin to thin out.
scholar_explanation: The instruction uses external spatial simplicity to induce internal attenuation of discursivity. A featureless or minimally differentiated field weakens the mind’s tendency toward object-construction; with the vilaya of mānasa-bhāva comes vṛtti-kṣaya. This is a classic tantric use of external ākāśa-like openness as a mirror for the dissolution of internal form-making.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Resting in the Middle Between Two Cognitions
sanskrit:
उभयोभाधियोऻाधने ध्यात्वा मध्यं समाश्रयेत् ।
युगऩच्च द्वयं त्यक्त्वा मध्ये तत्त्वं प्रकाशते ॥ ६१ ॥
transliteration:
ubhayobhādhi-yojñādhane dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet |
yugapac ca dvayaṃ tyaktvā madhye tattvaṃ prakāśate || 61 ||
translation: Meditating on the middle between the two states/cognitions, one should take refuge in the center. Abandoning both dual terms at once, the Reality (tattva) shines forth in the middle.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to notice the gap or center between two mental poles and rest there until reality reveals itself.
