beginner_explanation: Our mind usually swings between two sides: this and that, liking and disliking, inner and outer. This verse says to stop following either side and instead notice the quiet middle between them. In that pause, something deeper than ordinary thinking can become clear.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic madhya-upāya instruction: the yogin attends to the interval or center (madhya) between two vikalpas, bhāvas, or poles of cognition. By relinquishing dvaya, the binary structure of subject-object determination loosens, and tattva self-reveals. The verse resonates with Trika's valorization of the madhya as the locus of spanda and the direct opening to Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Holding the Gap After a Thought Dissolves
sanskrit:
भािे त्यिे वनरुद्धा वचन् नैि भािान्तरम् व्रजेत् ।
तदा तन्मध्यभािेन विकसत्यवत भािना ॥ ६२ ॥
transliteration:
bhāve tyakte niruddhā vā cetan naiva bhāvāntaram vrajet |
tadā tanmadhya-bhāvena vikasaty ati bhāvanā || 62 ||
translation: When a mental state (bhāva) is abandoned or restrained, if awareness does not move to another state, then through that middle condition there blossoms the supreme contemplative realization.
intent_summary: The verse instructs one to remain in awareness when one thought ends and before another begins, allowing deeper realization to unfold.
beginner_explanation: Usually, one thought ends and the next begins immediately. Bhairava says: when one thought stops, do not rush into another. Stay in that in-between moment, and a more open, alive awareness begins to appear.
scholar_explanation: The operative point is the non-transition into bhāvāntara: the yogin neither sustains a prior vṛtti nor permits immediate succession into another. The middle-state (tanmadhya-bhāva) becomes the site where parā-bhāvanā or expanded contemplative awareness unfolds spontaneously. This method reflects the VBT's repeated strategy of exploiting the interstice between mental modifications as an entry into nirvikalpa recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating Body or World as Consciousness
sanskrit:
सिं देहं वचन्मयं वह जगद्वा ऩवरभाियेत् ।
युगऩवन्नविधकल्पेन मनसा ऩरमोदय् ॥ ६३ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagad vā paribhāvayet |
yugapannirvikalpena manasā paramodayet || 63 ||
translation: One should contemplate the entire body, or the whole universe, as consisting of consciousness (cinmaya). With the mind made simultaneously free of conceptual division, the supreme awakening arises.
intent_summary: The verse teaches seeing both body and world as made of consciousness, so that nondual awakening can dawn.
beginner_explanation: We usually think consciousness is only inside our head. This verse invites you to feel that your whole body—and even the whole world—is made of awareness. When you stop dividing things into separate pieces, a profound openness can arise.
scholar_explanation: The practice expands cid-eka-rasa across both microcosm (deha) and macrocosm (jagat), dissolving the habitual distinction between embodied subject and external world. The phrase yugapan nirvikalpena indicates an immediate, non-sequential non-conceptual apprehension rather than an inferential metaphysics. This is quintessential Trika nondualism: all manifestation is cinmaya, and realization is recognition (pratyabhijñā) of that fact.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Awakening Through the Meeting of the Two Breaths
sanskrit:
िायुद्वयस्य सम्घट्टाद् अन्तर् िा िवहरन्तत् ।
योगी समत्वविऻानसमुद्गमनभाजनम् ॥ ६४ ॥
transliteration:
vāyu-dvayasya saṅghaṭṭād antar vā bahir antataḥ |
yogī samatva-vijñāna-samudgama-bhājanam || 64 ||
translation: From the meeting of the two breaths, either within or at the outer end, the yogin becomes the vessel for the arising of the knowledge of equanimity (samatva-vijñāna).
intent_summary: The verse teaches attending to the junction where inhalation and exhalation meet, allowing insight into fundamental equality or balance to arise.
beginner_explanation: Breathing has turning points: one at the end of the in-breath and one at the end of the out-breath. If you gently notice these meeting places, your mind can become balanced and still. From that balance, a deeper understanding opens.
scholar_explanation: Vāyu-dvaya refers to prāṇa and apāna, or more practically the in-breath and out-breath, whose saṅghaṭṭa is apprehended at the internal and external junctions. In these sandhis, discursivity weakens and samatva-vijñāna—knowledge of undifferentiated sameness or equilibrium—emerges. This aligns with numerous VBT breath dhāraṇās centered on kumbhaka-like transitional awareness rather than forceful prāṇāyāma.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Remembering the Body or World Filled With One's Own Bliss
sanskrit:
सिं जगत्स्वदेहं िा स्वानन्दभवरतं स्मरेत् ।
युगऩत्स्वामृतेनैि ऩरानन्दमयो भिेत् ॥ ६५ ॥
transliteration:
sarvaṃ jagat svadehaṃ vā svānanda-bharitaṃ smaret |
yugapat svāmṛtenaiva parānandamayo bhavet || 65 ||
translation: One should recollect the whole universe, or one's own body, as filled with one's own bliss. Simultaneously, by one's own nectar alone, one becomes pervaded by supreme bliss.
intent_summary: The verse teaches saturating body or world with one's innate bliss until one becomes established in supreme bliss.
beginner_explanation: Instead of looking for happiness outside, imagine that your own body—or even the whole world—is already filled with a gentle inner joy. Keep remembering it as if everything is soaked in that sweetness. Over time, that feeling can deepen into a much greater bliss.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā extends svānanda beyond the limited psychophysical self into totalized embodiment or cosmization. The phrase svāmṛtena suggests the innate nectar of consciousness-bliss rather than pleasure dependent on objects. It stands at the intersection of bhāvanā and recognition: the contemplative 'filling' culminates in parānandamayatā, identity with supreme bliss-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Immediate Great Bliss Through Secret Method
sanskrit:
कुहनेन प्रयोगेण सद्य एि मृगेऺणे ।
समुदेवत महानन्दो येन तत्त्वम् प्रकाशते ॥ ६६ ॥
transliteration:
kuhanena prayogeṇa sadya eva mṛgekṣaṇe |
samudevati mahānando yena tattvaṃ prakāśate || 66 ||
translation: By a secret application, O doe-eyed one, great bliss arises immediately; through it, the Reality (tattva) is revealed.
intent_summary: The verse points to a hidden experiential method in which sudden bliss becomes the doorway to direct revelation of reality.
beginner_explanation: Some experiences can suddenly open a person beyond ordinary thinking. Bhairava says there is a subtle or secret way to use such a moment of intense joy so that it reveals something ultimate. The key point is not the pleasure itself, but the truth it uncovers.
scholar_explanation: The verse is deliberately elliptical: kuhanena prayogena indicates an esoteric or concealed technique, likely clarified by adjacent verses involving embodied bliss and śakti-experience. Mahānanda here is not merely affective pleasure but an intensified opening in which tattva-prakāśa occurs. As elsewhere in the VBT, a peak experiential state is to be transmuted into recognition rather than pursued as an end in itself.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Blocking the Channels and Raising Prāṇa
sanskrit:
सिधस्रोतोवनिन्धेन प्राणशक्त्योर्ध्वधया शनै् ।
वऩऩीऱस्पशधिेऱायां प्रथते ऩरमं सुखम् ॥ ६७ ॥
transliteration:
sarva-srotovinirodhena prāṇa-śakty-ūrdhvayā śanaiḥ |
pipīla-sparśa-velāyāṃ prathate paramaṃ sukham || 67 ||
translation: By obstructing all the channels and gradually raising the power of prāṇa upward, at the moment of an ant-like tingling touch, supreme bliss unfolds.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that by restraining sensory or energetic outlets and gradually lifting prāṇa upward, a subtle inner sensation can open into supreme bliss.
beginner_explanation: If energy is no longer leaking outward and is gently drawn upward, you may notice a fine tingling or crawling sensation, like an ant moving on the skin. This verse says to pay attention at that moment, because it can become a doorway into deep joy. The practice is subtle and should be approached carefully and calmly.
scholar_explanation: Sarva-srotovinirodha may indicate sealing the bodily apertures, restraining sensory dispersion, or an internalized energetic closure akin to mudrā-bandha praxis. Prāṇa-śakti is raised upward gradually (śanaiḥ), and the pipīla-sparśa serves as a phenomenological marker of ascending kuṇḍalinī-like movement or subtle nāḍī activation. The culmination is parama-sukha, not as bodily sensation alone, but as consciousness disclosed through refined energetic ascent.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Placing the Mind in Bliss Within Fire and Poison
sanskrit:
िह्नेविधषस्य मध्ये तु वचत्तं सुखमयं वऺऩेत् ।
केिऱं िायुऩूणं िा स्मरानन्देन युज्यते ॥ ६८ ॥
transliteration:
vahner viṣasya madhye tu cittaṃ sukhamayaṃ kṣipet |
kevalaṃ vāyu-pūrṇaṃ vā smarānandena yujyate || 68 ||
translation: One should cast the mind, as filled with bliss, into the midst of fire or poison; or into that which is merely full of air. Thus one becomes united with the bliss of remembrance.
intent_summary: The verse teaches placing awareness into extreme or unstable conditions while retaining blissful cognition, thereby transforming shock or emptiness into contemplative bliss.
beginner_explanation: This is not an invitation to harm yourself. The deeper point is that even in intense, frightening, or unstable experiences, you can place the mind into a steady field of inner ease instead of panic. When that happens, even difficult situations can reveal a deeper peace.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of fire, poison, and air-filled emptiness is characteristic of the VBT's transgressive contemplative style: liminal or threatening conditions are alchemized through citta-sukhamayatā. Smarānanda may imply bliss born of sustained contemplative recollection, or erotic-memory bliss depending on interpretive context and neighboring verses. In either case, the soteriological move is the same: reframe affective intensity into a portal of absorptive awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Recognizing Bliss at the Union of Śakti
sanskrit:
शविसंगमसंऺुब्धशक्त्यािेशािसावनकम् ।
यत्सुखम् ब्रह्मतत्त्वस्य तत्सुखम् स्वाक्यमुच्यते ॥ ६९ ॥
transliteration:
śakti-saṅgama-saṃkṣubdha-śaktyāveśāvasānikam |
yat sukhaṃ brahma-tattvasya tat sukhaṃ svākyam ucyate || 69 ||
translation: The bliss that comes at the culmination of absorption into Śakti, stirred by the union with Śakti—that bliss is said to be the very bliss of Brahman-reality, one's own true utterance/inner declaration.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that the climax of energized union, when entered consciously, reveals a bliss identical with Brahman.
beginner_explanation: A very intense moment of energy, closeness, or union can briefly dissolve the usual sense of separation. Bhairava says that if recognized rightly, the bliss in that moment is not ordinary pleasure but a glimpse of the deepest reality. The important thing is awareness within the experience, not just chasing sensation.
scholar_explanation: This verse belongs to the VBT's cluster of erotic and śākta transmutation practices. Śakti-saṅgama and śaktyāveśa point not merely to sexual union in a physical sense, but to the penetrative influx of dynamic consciousness-power whose culminating sukha is identified with brahma-tattva. The claim is radically nondual: the apex of embodied bliss, stripped of grasping and recognized in its essence, is none other than the self-revelation of absolute consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss Through Memory Even Without the Śakti-Presence
sanskrit:
ऱेहनामन्थनाकोटै् स्त्रीसुखस्य भरात्स्मृते् ।
शक्त्यभािेऽवऩ देिेवश भिेदानन्दसम्प्लि् ॥ ७० ॥
transliteration:
lehanāmanthanākoṭaiḥ strī-sukhasya bharāt smṛteḥ |
śakty-abhāve 'pi deveśi bhaved ānanda-samplavaḥ || 70 ||
translation: Through kissing, rubbing, and countless modes of erotic delight—or through the fullness of remembering such pleasure—even in the absence of the Śakti-partner, O Goddess, there can arise a flood of bliss.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that even remembered or internalized erotic bliss can become a contemplative means to overwhelming spiritual bliss.
beginner_explanation: This verse says that a powerful memory of intimacy can affect the mind deeply, even when the other person is not present. Rather than being trapped in fantasy, the practitioner is meant to notice the raw energy and bliss itself. That energy can then be turned inward toward spiritual realization.
scholar_explanation: The verse extends the previous śākta-erotic dhāraṇā from actual relational contact to smṛti-mediated internalization. Śakty-abhāve does not negate the śakti-principle metaphysically; rather, it indicates that the experiential current can be invoked even without the external partner. In Trika terms, the erotic rasa is abstracted from object-dependence and recognized as one's own ānanda-śakti, capable of overflowing into contemplative absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the Surge of Great Joy
sanskrit:
आनन्दे महवत प्राप्ते दृष्टे िा िान्धिे वचरात् ।
आनन्दमुद्गतम् ध्यात्वा तल्लयस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ७१ ॥
transliteration:
ānande mahati prāpte dṛṣṭe vā bāndhave cirāt |
ānandam udyataṃ dhyātvā tallayas tanmanā bhavet || 71 ||
translation: When great joy arises, or when a dear relative/friend is seen after a long time, one should meditate on the upsurging bliss. By dissolving into that, one becomes absorbed in it; the mind becomes of that very nature.
intent_summary: Use a naturally arising wave of intense joy as the immediate object of meditation until the mind dissolves into that bliss.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes happiness suddenly bursts open in you—like meeting someone beloved after a long separation. Instead of just enjoying it casually, pause and notice the feeling itself. Rest in that joy so fully that thinking fades and only the feeling-presence remains.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā takes spontaneous ānanda as the gateway rather than manufactured concentration. The practitioner attends not to the external cause (the beloved person) but to the उद्गत/udyata ānanda arising in consciousness, allowing citta to enter laya in that affective expansion. It reflects the Trika principle that any intense vṛtti, if divested of objecthood and recognized at its source, becomes a portal to Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Bliss Through Savoring Food and Drink
sanskrit:
जववधऩानकृतोल्लासरसानन्दविजृम्भणात् ।
भाियेद्भवरतािस्थां महानन्दस्ततो भिेत् ॥ ७२ ॥
transliteration:
javavidhapāna-kṛtollāsa-rasānanda-vijṛmbhaṇāt |
bhāvayed bharitāvasthāṃ mahānandas tato bhavet || 72 ||
translation: From the expansion of delight and bliss produced by tasting food and drink, one should contemplate the state of being filled to fullness. From that, great bliss arises.
intent_summary: Use the pleasure of savoring taste as a doorway to the inner state of fullness and expansive bliss.
beginner_explanation: When eating or drinking something delightful, pay attention to the feeling of satisfaction spreading through you. Don’t stop at the taste on the tongue—notice the deeper sense of fullness it awakens. Rest in that fullness, and it can open into a more profound happiness.
scholar_explanation: The verse points to rasa as contemplative support: sensory relish becomes transmuted into bharitāvasthā, the state of plenitude or inner filledness. Rather than indulgence in viṣaya, the practice redirects gustatory enjoyment into awareness of the all-pervading ānanda underlying experience. This accords with the Kaula/Trika insight that bhoga, rightly recognized, is not opposed to yoga but can mature into mahānanda.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Identity with the Happiness of Sensory Enjoyment
sanskrit:
वगतावदविषयास्वादासमसौख्यैकतात्मन् ।
योवगनस्तन्मयत्वेन मनोरूढेस् तदात्मता ॥ ७३ ॥
transliteration:
gītādi-viṣayāsvāda-sama-saukhyaika-tātman |
yoginas tanmayatvena manorūḍhes tadātmatā || 73 ||
translation: In the enjoyment of objects such as song and the like, when there is a unified essence of happiness, the yogin, by becoming completely one with that, and when the mind is established there, attains identity with That.
intent_summary: Enter so completely into the pure happiness present in aesthetic or sensory enjoyment that the mind becomes one with its deeper source.
beginner_explanation: Beautiful music, art, or any refined pleasure can make you forget yourself for a moment. This teaching says to notice the happiness inside that moment and merge with it completely. When you stop separating “me” from “the experience,” a deeper identity is revealed.
scholar_explanation: The phrase gītādi-viṣayāsvāda indicates aesthetic and sensory relish, yet the operative focus is sama-saukhya-eka-tātman—the unitary essence of happiness present there. Through tanmayatā and manorūḍhi, the yogin shifts from object-enjoyment to identity with the underlying conscious bliss, culminating in tadātmatā. The verse resonates with Pratyabhijñā aesthetics, where rasa and camatkāra can disclose universalized consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fixing the Mind Wherever Satisfaction Arises
sanskrit:
यि यि मनस्तुवष्टमधनस्तिैि धारयेत् ।
ति ति ऩरानन्दस्वारूऩं सम्प्रितधते ॥ ७४ ॥
transliteration:
yatra yatra manas tuṣṭir manas tatraiva dhārayet |
tatra tatra parānanda-svarūpaṃ sampravartate || 74 ||
translation: Wherever the mind finds satisfaction, there one should hold it steadily. In each such place, the very nature of supreme bliss begins to unfold.
intent_summary: Whenever contentment naturally appears, stabilize attention there and let it reveal supreme bliss.
beginner_explanation: Any moment of genuine contentment can become meditation. When the mind feels quietly pleased or settled, stay with that feeling instead of moving on to the next thing. That simple satisfaction can deepen into a much greater peace and joy.
scholar_explanation: This is a generalized contemplative principle: tuṣṭi itself is the support of dhāraṇā. By stabilizing manas in the very locus of satisfaction rather than in the object that occasioned it, parānanda-svarūpa manifests. The verse broadens the affective methods by asserting that ordinary moments of fulfillment contain the vibratory signature of Bhairava when non-discursively sustained.

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Threshold Before Sleep
sanskrit:
अनागतायां वनद्रायां प्रणष्टे िाह्यगोचरे ।
सािस्था मनसा गम्या ऩरा देिी प्रकाशते ॥ ७५ ॥
transliteration:
anāgatāyāṃ nidrāyāṃ praṇaṣṭe bāhyagocare |
sāvasthā manasā gamyā parā devī prakāśate || 75 ||
translation: When sleep has not yet come, and the field of external objects has disappeared, that state is to be entered by the mind; then the Supreme Goddess shines forth.
intent_summary: Attend carefully to the transitional state just before sleep, after outer perception fades but before unconscious sleep begins.
beginner_explanation: There is a special moment right before sleep when the outside world drops away, but you are not fully asleep yet. This verse says to notice that in-between state. If you remain aware there, a deeper inner presence can reveal itself.
scholar_explanation: This liminal state—between jāgrat and nidrā—is a classic sandhi suitable for recognition practice. With bāhyagocara dissolved but sleep not yet actualized, the practitioner turns manas toward that subtle avasthā in which Parā Devī, the luminous ground of awareness, becomes evident. It parallels other VBT threshold practices where transitions expose the non-contracted nature of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing into Sky-Like Radiance
sanskrit:
तेजसा सूयधदीऩादेराकाशे शिऱीकृते ।
दृवष्टवनधिेश्या तिैि स्वात्मरूऩं प्रकाशते ॥ ७६ ॥
transliteration:
tejasā sūrya-dīpāder ākāśe śabalīkṛte |
dṛṣṭir niveśyā tatraiva svātmarūpaṃ prakāśate || 76 ||
translation: When space is variegated or suffused by the radiance of the sun, a lamp, or the like, one should place the gaze there. Right there, one’s own true nature shines forth.
intent_summary: Fix the gaze in luminous space—such as light-filled sky or radiance from a lamp—until the Self reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: Look steadily into open space lit by sunlight, a lamp, or another soft brightness. Instead of focusing on objects, attend to the glowing field itself. In that open seeing, your deeper nature may become clear.
scholar_explanation: The practice uses a luminous visual field as support: ākāśa śabalīkṛta by tejas becomes an exteriorized analogue of the inner chidakāśa. By niveśa of dṛṣṭi into the radiant expanse, the duality of seer and seen attenuates, and svātmarūpa manifests. This is akin to tantric forms of sky-gazing and jyoti-dhāraṇā, though the goal is not the light as object but Self-revelation through visual de-objectification.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fierce Gaze of Bhairavī
sanskrit:
करवङ्कण्या क्रोधनया भैरव्या ऱेवऱहानया ।
खेचयाध दृवष्टकाऱे च ऩरािावप्त् प्रकाशते ॥ ७७ ॥
transliteration:
karaṅkiṇyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā | 
khecaryā dṛṣṭikāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate || 77 ||
translation: At the time of the gaze of Bhairavī—fierce, wrathful, devouring/flame-licking, moving in space (khecarī)—the attainment of the Supreme shines forth.
intent_summary: Assume or contemplate the fierce, expansive, Bhairavī-like gaze until supreme realization flashes forth.
beginner_explanation: This verse points to a powerful, intense way of looking—not ordinary seeing, but a fierce, open, penetrating gaze. It is like looking so completely that hesitation drops away. In that intensity, something beyond the usual mind can appear.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes esoteric imagery of Bhairavī: krodhanā, lelihānā, and khecarī suggest a transgressive, upward-moving, devouring śakti rather than a merely visual technique. Dṛṣṭi here may refer both to an actual yogic gaze and to śaktipāta-like visionary intensity. Parāvāptiḥ, attainment of the Supreme, emerges when consciousness assumes the uncontracted, fierce mode of Bhairavī rather than the domesticated stance of ordinary perception.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fullness Through Unsupported Limbs
sanskrit:
मृद्वासने विजैकेन हस्तऩादौ वनराश्रयम् ।
वनधाय तत्प्रसङ्गेन ऩरा ऩूणाध मवतभधिेत् ॥ ७८ ॥
transliteration:
mṛdv-āsane sphij-aikena hastapādau nirāśrayam | 
nidhāya tat-prasaṅgena parā pūrṇā matir bhavet || 78 ||
translation: Seated on a soft seat, with only the buttocks supported, and placing the hands and feet without support, through that condition the mind becomes supremely full.
intent_summary: Adopt a poised bodily position in which the body is minimally supported, and let that unstable openness evoke a state of inner fullness.
beginner_explanation: Sit gently so that mainly your seat touches the cushion, while the hands and feet are not leaning or braced. This creates a subtle sense of balance and alertness. Staying with that feeling can gather the mind into a clear, full presence.
scholar_explanation: This posture-based dhāraṇā exploits nirāśraya at the bodily level to induce a corresponding non-dependence in cognition. With the body delicately balanced on a soft seat, habitual supports are reduced, and mati expands into parā pūrṇatā. The verse illustrates the Trika principle that refined proprioceptive conditions can catalyze entry into the supportless ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Peace Through Contracted Arms and Armpit Focus
sanskrit:
उऩविश्यासने सम्यविाहू कृत्वाधधकुवञ्चतौ ।
कऺव्योवि मन् कुिधन् शममायावत तल्लयात् ॥ ७९ ॥
transliteration:
upaviśy āsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdha-kuñcitau | 
kakṣa-vyomni manaḥ kurvan śamam āyāti tallayāt || 79 ||
translation: Sitting properly in a seat, making the arms half-bent, and placing the mind in the space of the armpits, one comes to peace through absorption in that.
intent_summary: Sit steadily, hold the arms in a specific bent posture, and focus attention in the subtle space of the armpits until the mind becomes peaceful.
beginner_explanation: Sit upright and bend the arms slightly. Then bring attention to the inner space in the armpit area, as if noticing a quiet hollow there. This unusual focus can calm the mind and draw it into stillness.
scholar_explanation: The kakṣa-vyoman, the ‘space’ of the armpits, functions here as a subtle bodily cavity for dhāraṇā. Through localized attention and laya, śama arises—not merely relaxation, but pacification of mental movement. Such somatic-space practices are characteristic of the VBT’s use of embodied micro-loci as portals into expansive awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steady Gaze on a Gross Form
sanskrit:
स्थूऱरूऩस्य भािस्य स्तब्धां दृवष्टं वनऩात्य च ।
अवचरेण वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा वशिं व्रजेत् ॥ ८० ॥
transliteration:
sthūlarūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātya ca | 
acireṇa nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā śivaṃ vrajet || 80 ||
translation: Fixing an unmoving gaze upon a gross form or object, one soon makes the mind supportless; thus one attains Śiva.
intent_summary: Steadily gaze at a physical object until ordinary mental supports fall away and the mind opens into the supportless state.
beginner_explanation: Choose a simple visible object and look at it without shifting your eyes much. If you stay steady, the mind’s usual chatter can lose its grip. Then awareness opens beyond the object into a deeper stillness.
scholar_explanation: This is a form of visual fixation akin to trataka, but its telos is nirādhāra-manas, the supportless mind. The sthūlarūpa is only an initial support; by immobilizing dṛṣṭi, discursive fluctuation subsides and consciousness disengages from object-dependence, culminating in Śiva-realization. The movement from support to supportlessness is paradigmatic of many VBT dhāraṇās.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Awareness Placed in the Mouth's Middle with Subtle Utterance
sanskrit:
मध्यवजह्वे िावरतास्ये मध्ये वनवऺप्य चेतनाम् ।
होच्चारं मनसा कुिंस्तत् शान्ते प्रऱीयते ॥ ८१ ॥
transliteration:
madhya-vahneḥ vā varatāsye madhye vinikṣipya cetanām |
hoccāraṃ manasā kurvan tat śānte pralīyate || 81 ||
translation: Placing awareness in the middle of the mouth—or at the central channel of utterance—and performing the subtle exclamation/utterness (uccāra) mentally, one dissolves into that peace when the sound comes to rest.
intent_summary: It teaches the practitioner to place awareness in the inner locus of sound and follow mental utterance into the silence where consciousness dissolves.
beginner_explanation: Bring your attention to the inside of the mouth, especially the subtle place where sound seems to begin. Then very gently make the sound inwardly, only in the mind, and notice what remains when it fades. The practice is less about the sound itself and more about the quiet after it ends.
scholar_explanation: This verse points to mānasika uccāra: the internalized emergence and reabsorption of sound-vibration in the madhya, the 'middle.' In Trika terms, one attends not merely to articulated phoneme but to the spanda of śabda as it resolves into śānti, the silent ground of consciousness. It resonates with other VBT methods in which the junction or cessation of movement reveals Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the Unsupported Body
sanskrit:
आसने शयने वस्थत्वा वनराधारं विभाियन् ।
स्वदेहं मनवस वऺणे ऺणात्क्षीणाशयो भिेत् ॥ ८२ ॥
transliteration:
āsane śayane sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan |
svadehaṃ manasi kṣiṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet || 82 ||
translation: Whether seated or lying down, contemplating supportlessness (nirādhāra), and letting one's own body be attenuated in the mind, one quickly becomes one whose latent mental tendencies are exhausted.
intent_summary: It instructs the practitioner to contemplate the body as unsupported and mentally insubstantial so that deep conditioning loses its hold.
beginner_explanation: Sit or lie down and imagine that your body is not resting on anything solid. Let the usual feeling of heaviness and fixedness soften in the mind. As the sense of physical certainty loosens, old mental habits can briefly lose their grip too.
scholar_explanation: The key term nirādhāra suggests not only 'without support' physically but unsupported by conceptual fixation. By thinning out the mental construction of svadeha, the practitioner undermines āśaya—latent deposits or karmic tendencies embedded in citta. The verse aligns with Trika's deconstruction of embodiment as contracted consciousness rather than an ultimately separate material fact.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Stilling the Mind Through Gradual Cessation of Bodily Movement
sanskrit:
चऱासने वस्थतस्याथ शनैिाध देहचाऱनात् ।
प्रशान्ते मानसे भािे देवि वदव्यौघम् आप्नुयात् ॥ ८३ ॥
transliteration:
calāsane sthitasyātha śanair vā deha-cālanāt |
praśānte mānase bhāve devi divyaugham āpnuyāt || 83 ||
translation: When one is seated on a moving seat—or by gradually ceasing bodily movement—then, O Devi, when the mental state becomes peaceful, one attains a divine influx (divyaugha).
intent_summary: It teaches that by observing motion and then allowing bodily movement to settle, the mind becomes quiet and opens to a descending current of higher awareness.
beginner_explanation: You can notice this when rocking, swaying, or moving slightly and then slowly becoming still. As the body settles, the mind often settles with it. In that quiet, a subtle sense of openness or uplift may appear on its own.
scholar_explanation: The verse hinges on the relation between deha-cālana and mānasa-bhāva: movement, when consciously resolved into stillness, reveals a non-discursive state. Divyaugha may be read as the descent or manifestation of a divine current, akin to śaktipāta or a spontaneous unveiling of heightened awareness. The method uses kinesthetic transition as a gateway to praśānta-citta.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Steady Gaze into the Stainless Sky
sanskrit:
आकाशं विमऱं ऩश्यन्कृत्वा दृवष्टं वनरन्तराम् ।
स्तब्धात्मा तत्क्षणाद्देवि भैरिं िऩुराप्नुयात् ॥ ८४ ॥
transliteration:
ākāśaṃ vimalaṃ paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantarām |
stabdhātmā tat-kṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt || 84 ||
translation: Gazing at the stainless sky with an unbroken stare, becoming inwardly still, one at that very moment, O Devi, attains the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: It instructs the practitioner to use uninterrupted sky-gazing to enter inner stillness and recognize Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Look into a clear open sky without jumping from object to object. Let the eyes become steady and the mind stop chasing thoughts. The openness outside can help you discover a similar openness inside.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic ākāśa-dhāraṇā in which the external vimala ākāśa serves as a support for entry into inner vastness. The phrase stabdhātmā indicates a suspension of mental fluctuation, not inertness but poised awareness. To 'attain the body of Bhairava' signifies recognition (pratyabhijñā) of consciousness as all-pervasive and unconfined like space.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Absorbing the Cosmos as Bhairava in the Sky
sanskrit:
ऱीनं मूवनध वियत्सिधम् भैरित्वेन भाियेत् ।
तत्सिधम् भैरिाकारतेजस्तत्त्वं समाविशेत् ॥ ८५ ॥
transliteration:
līnaṃ mūrdhni viyat-sarvaṃ bhairavatvena bhāvayet |
tat-sarvaṃ bhairavākāra-tejas-tattvaṃ samāviśet || 85 ||
translation: One should contemplate the entire expanse of space, gathered and absorbed above/in the crown, as Bhairava himself. Then one enters into that whole reality as the radiant essence whose form is Bhairava.
intent_summary: It teaches the practitioner to perceive the total expanse of space as Bhairava and merge into its radiant essence.
beginner_explanation: Instead of seeing space as empty and separate, imagine all openness as a living divine presence. Let that vastness gather into a single felt reality and then allow yourself to merge with it. The aim is to stop feeling like a small observer standing outside the universe.
scholar_explanation: This verse intensifies the prior ākāśa practice by explicitly sacralizing viyat as Bhairava. The movement is from bhāvanā ('contemplative envisioning') to samāveśa, immersive entry into bhairavākāra-tejas-tattva, the luminous ontological essence of Bhairava. It exemplifies Trika nondual theology wherein apparent spatial extension is recognized as cit-śakti's self-expression.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing the World as Bhairava's Infinite Light
sanskrit:
वकवञ्चज्ज्ञातम् द्वैतदावय िाह्याऱोकस्तम् ऩुन् ।
विश्वावद भैरिं रूऩं ऻात्वानन्तप्रकाशभृत् ॥ ८६ ॥
transliteration:
kiñcij jñātaṃ dvaitadāyi bāhyālokaḥ tamas punaḥ |
viśvād bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ jñātvā ananta-prakāśa-bhṛt || 86 ||
translation: Whatever is known as something limited gives rise to duality; external light too is again obscuring darkness. But knowing the universe as the form of Bhairava, one becomes the bearer of infinite light.
intent_summary: It teaches that object-based knowing and ordinary external perception are limited, while recognizing the whole universe as Bhairava reveals infinite luminosity.
beginner_explanation: When you focus on separate things, the mind divides reality into 'me' and 'that.' This verse says even ordinary seeing can keep us on the surface. But if everything is recognized as one living presence, awareness feels vast and bright instead of split up.
scholar_explanation: The verse contrasts kiñcid-jñāna, fragmentary cognition that produces dvaita, with the recognition of viśva as Bhairava-rūpa. The striking claim that bāhyāloka is 'darkness' underscores that sensory objectivity, though luminous in appearance, conceals the ananta-prakāśa of self-revealing consciousness. This is quintessential Pratyabhijñā metaphysics: true light is not physical illumination but cit-prakāśa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating Darkness on the Night of the Dark Fortnight
sanskrit:
एिमेि दुवनधशायां कृष्णऩऺागमे वचरम् ।
तैवमरं भाियन् रूऩं भैरिं रूऩमेष्यवत ॥ ८७ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva durniśāyāṃ kṛṣṇa-pakṣāgame ciram |
taimiraṃ bhāvayan rūpaṃ bhairavaṃ rūpam eṣyati || 87 ||
translation: In just this way, on a dark night during the waning fortnight, by contemplating darkness for a long time, one attains the form of Bhairava.
intent_summary: It instructs the practitioner to meditate steadily on external darkness until it reveals Bhairava-consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Sit in deep darkness, especially on a moonless or very dark night, and simply remain with the experience of dark space. If you do not resist it or fill it with imagination, the darkness can become strangely alive and spacious. The practice is to let darkness open into presence rather than fear.
scholar_explanation: Taimira here functions as a contemplative support parallel to ākāśa: darkness is not mere absence but an undifferentiated field in which object-formation subsides. The verse strategically uses the kṛṣṇa-pakṣa environment to reduce sensory differentiation, facilitating entry into Bhairava-rūpa. As in other Trika methods, the apparent negation of phenomena becomes a portal to nondual revelation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Inner Dark Behind Closed Eyes
sanskrit:
एिमेि वनमील्यादौ नेिे कृष्णाभमाग्रत् ।
प्रसायध भैरिं रूऩं भाियम्स्तन्मयो भिेत् ॥ ८८ ॥
transliteration:
evam eva nimīlyādau netre kṛṣṇābham agrataḥ |
prasārya bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ bhāvayan tanmayo bhavet || 88 ||
translation: Likewise, at first closing the eyes and seeing the dark appearance before oneself, extending that into the form of Bhairava through contemplation, one becomes one with that.
intent_summary: It teaches the practitioner to use the inner darkness seen with closed eyes as a gateway to identification with Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Close your eyes and notice the dark field that appears in front of you. Instead of ignoring it, let it spread into a vast presence. Over time, the darkness is no longer just blankness; it becomes a doorway into a deeper sense of being.
scholar_explanation: This internalizes the preceding darkness practice: the kṛṣṇābha visual field behind closed eyes becomes the support for bhāvanā. The verb prasārya suggests expanding the limited inner dark into the all-pervasive Bhairava-rūpa, culminating in tanmayatā, complete identity with the contemplated reality. The verse is a subtle bridge between visualization and nondual absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Revelation of the Self in the Gap of Sensory Interruption
sanskrit:
यस्य कस्येवन्द्रयस्यावऩ व्याघाताच्च वनरोधत् ।
प्रविष्टस्याद्वये शून्ये तिैिात्मा प्रकाशते ॥ ८९ ॥
transliteration:
yasya kasyendriyasyāpi vyāghātāc ca nirodhataḥ |
praviṣṭasyādvaye śūnye tatraivātmā prakāśate || 89 ||
translation: By the interruption or stopping of any one of the senses, when one enters the nondual void, there itself the Self shines forth.
intent_summary: It teaches that when sensory activity is suddenly interrupted and one enters the gap beyond dualistic perception, the Self is directly revealed.
beginner_explanation: If any sense suddenly stops or is cut off, there can be a brief gap before the mind fills it in again. This verse says that gap is very important. In that opening, you may notice a simple aware presence that does not depend on seeing, hearing, or touching.
scholar_explanation: The operative moment is indriya-vyāghāta or nirodha, the arrest of ordinary sensory functioning. What becomes accessible is advaya-śūnya, not nihilistic emptiness but the nondual interval in which ātmā self-manifests as prakāśa. This accords with the VBT's recurring use of junctions, breaks, and liminal disruptions as privileged sites of recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Japa of the Letter A Without Bindu or Visarga
sanskrit:
अविन्दुम् अविसगधम् च अकारम् जऩतो महान् ।
उदेवत देवि सहसा ऻानौघ् ऩरमेश्वर् ॥ ९० ॥
transliteration:
abindum avisargaṃ ca akāraṃ japato mahān |
udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ || 90 ||
translation: For one who repeats the phoneme 'A' without bindu and without visarga, O Devi, there suddenly arises the great flood of knowledge—Parameśvara himself.
intent_summary: It teaches the practitioner to recite the pure sound 'A' in its unmodified form so that a sudden surge of divine knowledge may arise.
beginner_explanation: Use the simplest open sound, 'A,' without adding anything extra at the end. Repeat it with full attention until the sound feels pure and open. The verse says this can trigger a sudden breakthrough into clear knowing.
scholar_explanation: Akāra is the primal phoneme in many Śaiva and Tantric systems, often associated with anuttara, the unsurpassable ground. Here its recitation devoid of bindu and visarga points to the unelaborated source of manifestation prior to differentiation. The arising of jñānaugha as Parameśvara indicates that mantra, reduced to its most fundamental vibration, discloses the supreme as immediate self-luminous awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: From Visarga Sound to the Eternal Brahman
sanskrit:
िणधस्य सविसगधस्य विसगाधन्तं वचवतं कुरु ।
वनराधारेण वचत्तेन स्पृशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ९१ ॥
transliteration:
bindhasya savisargasya visargāntaṃ vicintayet |
antar-ādhāreṇa cittena spṛśed brahma sanātanam || 91 ||
translation: One should contemplate the terminal point of the sound marked by visarga (ḥ), together with bindu. With the mind supported inwardly, one touches the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to trace a subtle phonemic vibration to its point of cessation and thereby enter the eternal ground of consciousness.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses a very subtle sound, especially the fading end of a breathy syllable, as a doorway inward. Instead of following the sound outward, you notice where it disappears. Resting attention there can reveal a quiet, timeless presence beneath thought.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes bindu and visarga, both central in Tantric phonemic metaphysics, as liminal points where manifest śabda returns to its source. The instruction is not merely phonetic but ontological: by attending to visargānta, the practitioner follows vāṇī back into parā-vāk and touches sanātana-brahman. This aligns with VBT methods that exploit the junction between expression and dissolution.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditating on the Self as Sky-Like
sanskrit:
व्योमाकारं स्वमात्मानम् ध्यायेवद्दवग्भरनािृतम् ।
वनराश्रया वचवत् शवि् स्वरूऩं दशधयेत्तदा ॥ ९२ ॥
transliteration:
vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānaṃ dhyāyed digbhir anāvṛtam |
nirāśrayā cid-rūpā śaktiḥ svarūpaṃ darśayet tadā || 92 ||
translation: One should meditate on one's own Self as having the form of space, unobstructed by the directions. Then the supportless power whose nature is consciousness reveals its true form.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to contemplate the Self as boundless space so that unsupported consciousness-power may reveal itself directly.
beginner_explanation: Imagine your real nature not as a small person inside the body, but as open sky with no walls. Nothing limits it, and it does not depend on anything to hold it up. When attention relaxes into that openness, a deeper sense of living awareness can show itself.
scholar_explanation: Here the ātman is visualized as vyomākāra, sky-like and directionless, evoking cidākāśa rather than gross physical space. The phrase nirāśrayā śaktiḥ suggests autonomous cit-śakti, consciousness not grounded in objectivity or mental construction. This is a classic Śaiva move from spatial metaphor to recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's own unbounded svarūpa.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Piercing Sensation with One-Pointed Awareness
sanskrit:
वकंवचदङ्गम् विवभद्यादौ तीक्ष्णसूच्यावदना तत् ।
तिैि चेतनां युक्त्वा भैरिे वनमधऱा गवत् ॥ ९३ ॥
transliteration:
kiñcid aṅgaṃ vibhidyādau tīkṣṇa-sūcy-ādinā tataḥ |
tatraiva cetanāṃ yuktvā bhairave nirmalā gatiḥ || 93 ||
translation: If at first some part of the body is pierced by a sharp needle or the like, then fixing awareness precisely there, one attains a stainless movement into Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches using acute bodily sensation as a focal point through which awareness can become fully absorbed in Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: A sharp sensation instantly gathers the mind into one place. The instruction is to put full attention right into that point, without adding stories or resistance. If the attention becomes pure and steady, the sensation can open into a deeper stillness.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā uses intense tactile localization as an expedient means: pain, when divested of conceptual overlay, becomes a gateway to non-discursive absorption. The key is cetanā-yoga with the sensation itself, not aversion to it. Comparable to other VBT techniques, the limited sensation is transmuted into nirmalā gati, a purified entry into Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding Between the Beginning and End of Thought
sanskrit:
वचत्ताद्यन्त्कृवतनाधवस्त ममान्तभाधियेवदवत ।
विकल्पानामभािेन विकल्पैरुवितो भिेत् ॥ ९४ ॥
transliteration:
cittādyanta-kṛtinā dhyāyet mamāntar bhāvayed iti |
vikalpānām abhāvena vikalpair ujjhito bhavet || 94 ||
translation: One should contemplate the beginning and end of thought, reflecting, 'Within that is my inner reality.' Through the absence of conceptual constructions (vikalpa), one becomes free from conceptualization.
intent_summary: The verse points the practitioner to the gaps at the arising and subsiding of thought as a way to become free of conceptual activity.
beginner_explanation: Thoughts seem continuous, but each one begins and ends. This practice asks you to notice those tiny openings before a thought forms and after it fades. In those gaps, the mind is simpler, quieter, and less caught in mental chatter.
scholar_explanation: The instruction centers on citta's ādi and anta, the thresholds of mentation where vikalpa has not yet solidified or has already dissolved. To 'locate me within' indicates Bhairava as the non-conceptual ground immanent in thought's emergence and withdrawal. This resembles the Pratyabhijñā insight that vikalpa depends upon, but never obscures, self-luminous consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Seeing Māyā as Differentiating Power
sanskrit:
माया विमोवहनी नाम कऱाया् कऱनं वस्थतम् ।
इत्यावदधमं तत्त्वानां कऱयन्न ऩृथग्भिेत् ॥ ९५ ॥
transliteration:
māyā vimohinī nāma kalāyāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam |
ityādi-dharmaṃ tattvānāṃ kalayan na pṛthag bhavet || 95 ||
translation: That which is called māyā, the deluding power, consists in the measuring-out activity of kalā. When one contemplates the categories (tattvas) together with their properties such as permanence and the rest, one does not remain separate from them.
intent_summary: The verse teaches insight into māyā as the differentiating power that measures out reality, leading beyond a separate relation to the tattvas.
beginner_explanation: Usually we divide life into many separate things and treat them as if they stand apart from us. This verse says that this dividing tendency is māyā, a power that breaks unity into pieces. By carefully seeing how all experiences are structured, you can stop feeling cut off from reality.
scholar_explanation: Māyā here is defined through kalana, the delimiting or measuring activity associated with kalā and the fragmentation of the undivided whole into tattvic differentiation. The practice is contemplative discernment: one examines the tattvas and their dharmas not to reinforce ontological separation but to see differentiation as a display of consciousness. Thus, analysis culminates in non-separation rather than dualistic metaphysics.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Returning Desire to Its Source
sanskrit:
झवगतीच्छां समुत्पन्नामिऱोक्य शमं नयेत् ।
यत एि समुद्भूता ततस्तिैि ऱीयते ॥ ९६ ॥
transliteration:
jagaty icchāṃ samutpannām ālokya śamaṃ nayet |
yata eva samudbhūtā tatas taiva līyate || 96 ||
translation: Observing a desire that has arisen in the world of experience, one should bring it to śānti (calmness). From wherever it has arisen, into that very place it dissolves again.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to observe desire at its arising and allow it to settle back into the source from which it emerged.
beginner_explanation: When a desire appears, instead of chasing it, look closely at it. Notice where it came from before it became a strong urge. If you stay with it calmly, the desire can sink back into the same inner space it came from.
scholar_explanation: Icchā is approached phenomenologically: not suppressed morally, but tracked to its point of origination and reabsorption. The verse reflects a Śaiva understanding that all movements arise from and subside into cit-śakti. By reversing the extroverted vector of desire, one discovers its source as consciousness itself.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Who Am I Before Desire or Knowledge Arises?
sanskrit:
यदा ममेच्छा नोत्पन्ना ऻानं िा कस्तदावस्म िै ।
तत्त्वतोऽहम् तथाभूतस्तल्लीनस्तन्मना भिेत् ॥ ९७ ॥
transliteration:
yadā mamecchā notpannā jñānaṃ vā kas tadāsmi vai |
tattvato'ham tathābhūtas tallīnas tanmanā bhavet || 97 ||
translation: When no desire has arisen in me, nor any knowledge—what indeed am I then? In truth, being of that nature, one should become absorbed in That, with the mind made of That.
intent_summary: The verse invites inquiry into the state prior to desire and cognition, leading to absorption in one's essential nature.
beginner_explanation: Before you want something, and before you label or understand anything, there is still a basic sense of being. This verse asks you to notice that simple existence directly. Resting there, the mind can merge into a more fundamental identity.
scholar_explanation: This is a radical pre-intentional inquiry into the condition prior to icchā and jñāna as differentiated functions. The question 'kas tadā asmi?' destabilizes empirical selfhood and turns attention toward the undivided aham of Bhairava. The final instruction points to tanmayatā and laya in the pre-conceptual ground of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Entering the Arising of Desire or Knowledge
sanskrit:
इच्छायामथिा ऻाने जाते वचत्तं वनिेशयेत् ।
आत्मिुद्ध्यानन्यचेतास्ततस्तत्त्वाथधदशधनम् ॥ ९८ ॥
transliteration:
icchāyām athavā jñāne jāte cittaṃ niveśayet |
ātma-buddhy-ananya-cetās tatas tattvārtha-darśanam || 98 ||
translation: When desire or knowledge arises, one should place the mind into that. With the understanding that it is the Self, and with consciousness not turned elsewhere, then there is vision of the true reality.
intent_summary: The verse teaches fully entering desire or cognition as expressions of the Self, thereby revealing true reality.
beginner_explanation: Instead of treating thoughts and desires as distractions, this practice says to enter them with full attention. But do so while remembering that the energy of the experience is not separate from your deeper being. Then even ordinary mental events can reveal something true and profound.
scholar_explanation: Unlike methods that privilege only cessation, this dhāraṇā sacralizes the arising of icchā and jñāna as modes of ātma-śakti. The crucial move is ātma-buddhi and ananya-cetas: one recognizes the event as non-other than consciousness. This is quintessentially non-dual Śaiva, where manifestation itself becomes the site of tattvārtha-darśana.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Knowledge Without Cause or Support
sanskrit:
वनवनधवमत्तं भिेज्ज्ञानम् वनराधारं भ्रमात्मकम् ।
तत्त्वत् कस्यवचन्नैतद् एिम्भािी वशि् वप्रये ॥ ९९ ॥
transliteration:
nirnimittaṃ bhavej jñānaṃ nirādhāraṃ bhramātmakam |
tattvataḥ kasyacin naitad evambhāvī śiva-priye || 99 ||
translation: Knowledge may appear causeless, without support, and of the nature of wandering illusion. Yet in truth it does not belong to anyone at all. One who abides thus, O priya of Śiva, [realizes the truth].
intent_summary: The verse undermines possessive identification with knowledge by revealing cognition as unsupported and not owned by any individual.
beginner_explanation: We usually think, 'My thoughts, my knowledge, my understanding.' This verse challenges that by saying knowledge can arise on its own, without a solid owner behind it. Seeing this loosens the sense of a separate thinker and opens a wider perspective.
scholar_explanation: The verse deconstructs epistemic ownership: jñāna is presented as nirnimitta and nirādhāra, lacking fixed causal or substantial grounding from the ego's perspective. The phrase tattvataḥ kasyacin na etat denies individuated proprietorship over cognition, echoing the Śaiva view that all knowing is a function of universal cit. 'Evambhāvī' indicates one established in this recognition rather than merely entertaining it conceptually.

speaker: Bhairava
title: One Conscious Dharma in All Bodies
sanskrit:
वचद्धमाध सिधदेहेषु विशेषो नावस्त कुिवचत् ।
अतश्च तन्मयं सिं भाियन्भिवजज्जन् ॥ १०० ॥
transliteration:
cid-dharmā sarva-deheṣu viśeṣo nāsti kutracit |
ataś ca tanmayaṃ sarvaṃ bhāvayan bhavajij janaḥ || 100 ||
translation: The nature of consciousness is present in all bodies; there is no distinction anywhere. Therefore, contemplating everything as consisting of That, a person becomes victorious over becoming (saṃsāra).
intent_summary: The verse teaches seeing the same consciousness in all beings and all forms, thereby transcending separative existence.
beginner_explanation: Although bodies look different, the basic fact of awareness is the same everywhere. If you practice seeing all life as filled with that one consciousness, the feeling of isolation starts to weaken. This can bring compassion, unity, and freedom from narrow identity.
scholar_explanation: Cid-dharma is declared universal across all embodied loci, denying any essential viśeṣa at the level of consciousness itself. The contemplative result is tanmayatā with sarva, a distinctly non-dual Bhairava-vision that sublates saṃsāric differentiation without denying phenomenal multiplicity. This resonates strongly with Trika notions of one cit manifesting as all pramātṛs and objects alike.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Transforming Passion into the Residual Reality
sanskrit:
कामक्रोधऱोभमोहमदमात्सयधगोचरे ।
िुवद्धं वनवस्तवमतां कृत्वा तत्तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०१ ॥
transliteration:
kāma-krodha-lobha-moha-mada-mātsarya-gocare |
buddhaṃ nivastava-matāṃ kṛtvā tat-tattvam avaśiṣyate || 101 ||
translation: Where desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy arise as objects of experience, making the awakened understanding rest there as insubstantial (or non-real), that Reality-thatness alone remains.
intent_summary: The verse teaches the practitioner to examine intense afflictive states so deeply that their unreal or constructed nature is seen, leaving only the underlying reality.
beginner_explanation: When strong emotions like anger or jealousy appear, do not get lost in the story. Look directly at the raw experience and see that it is unstable and not solid. As the mental drama loosens, a quieter and more basic awareness remains.
scholar_explanation: This verse works with the kleśa-like eruptions of kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, and mātsarya as immediate gateways rather than obstacles. By establishing buddhi in their avastava or asārata—their non-substantiality—the yogin lets the superimposed vikalpa-collapse occur, and tattva alone remains. It reflects the Bhairava-tantric strategy of transmuting bondage into upāya through penetrative recognition (pratyabhijñā).

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating the World as Magical Appearance
sanskrit:
इन्द्रजाऱमयं विश्वं व्यस्तं िा वचिकमधित् ।
भ्रमद्वा ध्यायत् सिं ऩश्यतश्च सुखोद्गम् ॥ १०२ ॥
transliteration:
indrajālamayaṃ viśvaṃ vyastaṃ vā citra-karmavat |
bhramad vā dhyāyat sarvaṃ paśyataś ca sukhodgamam || 102 ||
translation: Meditating on the universe as made of magic illusion (indrajāla), or as variegated like a painted display, or as whirling appearance—while seeing all in this way, one experiences the arising of bliss.
intent_summary: The verse instructs one to view the world as a marvelous but insubstantial display, which loosens fixation and opens into bliss.
beginner_explanation: Look at life as if it were a magical show or a vivid painting. Things still appear, but they no longer feel so heavy or absolute. This lighter way of seeing can bring a surprising sense of freedom and joy.
scholar_explanation: The imagery of indrajāla points to phenomenal manifestation as wondrous yet non-substantial, neither denied nor reified. Seeing the viśva as citra-karmavat or bhramat relocates attention from object-certainty to the play of appearing itself, facilitating ānanda through de-solidification of prameya. This aligns with Trika's understanding of the universe as Śiva's self-display (ābhāsa) rather than independently real multiplicity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding in the Middle Beyond Pleasure and Pain
sanskrit:
न वचत्तं वनवऺऩेद् दु्खे न सुखे िा ऩवरवऺऩेत् ।
भैरवि ऻायतां मध्ये वकं तत्त्वमिवशष्यते ॥ १०३ ॥
transliteration:
na cittaṃ nikṣiped duḥkhe na sukhe vā parikṣipet |
bhairavi jñāyatāṃ madhye kiṃ tattvam avaśiṣyate || 103 ||
translation: Do not cast the mind into duḥkha (pain), nor scatter it into pleasure. O Bhairavī, let the middle be known: what reality remains there?
intent_summary: The verse teaches resting neither in aversion nor attachment, but discovering the underlying reality in the balanced middle between them.
beginner_explanation: Usually the mind runs away from pain and clings to pleasure. Here the instruction is to do neither. Stay steady in between, and notice the deeper presence that is there before liking and disliking take over.
scholar_explanation: This is a classic madhya-upāya: neither duḥkha-dveṣa nor sukha-rāga is allowed to seize citta. In the interval free of affective polarization, tattva is directly intuited as the nondual ground of both experiences. The verse resonates with VBT's recurrent use of the middle point—between breaths, thoughts, sensations, or opposites—as the doorway to Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abiding as All-Pervading Presence Beyond the Body
sanskrit:
विहाय वनजदेहस्थं सिधिास्मीवत भाियन् ।
दृढेन मनसा दृष्ट्या नान्येवऺण्या सुखी भिेत् ॥ १०४ ॥
transliteration:
vihāya nijadehasthaṃ sarvatrāsmīti bhāvayan |
dṛḍhena manasā dṛṣṭyā nānyekṣiṇyā sukhī bhavet || 104 ||
translation: Abandoning identification with one's own body-location, and contemplating, “I am everywhere,” with firm mind and vision, not seeing anything as other, one becomes blissful.
intent_summary: The verse teaches expanding identity beyond the body and stabilizing the vision of non-separation from all that appears.
beginner_explanation: Instead of feeling that you are trapped inside one small body, imagine and sense that your being is everywhere. Hold that feeling steadily. As the sense of separation softens, a natural happiness appears.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā explicitly counters dehātma-buddhi by dislodging consciousness from nijadehastha limitation and establishing sarvatrāsmi-bhāvanā. The phrase nānyekṣiṇyā indicates a nondual vision in which no object is apprehended as truly other. It reflects the Trika doctrine that the self is not body-bound but the all-pervasive vimarśa of Paramaśiva.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contemplating Awareness in Pot and Self as All-Pervading
sanskrit:
घटादौ यच्च विऻानवमच्छाद्यं िा ममान्तरे ।
नैि सिधगतं जातं भाियवन्नवत सिधग् ॥ १०५ ॥
transliteration:
ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare |
naiva sarvagataṃ jātaṃ bhāvayann iti sarvagaḥ || 105 ||
translation: The awareness present in a pot and other objects, and that which appears within me as desire and so on—contemplating that it is not truly divided from the all-pervading, one becomes all-pervading.
intent_summary: The verse points the practitioner to recognize one undivided awareness in external objects and internal states alike.
beginner_explanation: Notice that knowing is present when you see an object outside and also when you feel something inside, like desire. This instruction asks you to sense that the same field of awareness is in both. When you stop splitting inner and outer, your sense of self becomes much wider.
scholar_explanation: Though the transmitted text is uncertain, the sense is clear: vijñāna in external loci such as ghaṭa and in internal modifications such as icchā is to be contemplated as non-separate from the sarvagata principle. This undermines the inner/outer bifurcation structuring ordinary cognition and reveals consciousness as equally immanent in pramātṛ, prameya, and mental vṛtti. It is a contemplative application of universalized cit rather than localized subjectivity.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Attentiveness to the Relation of Knower and Known
sanskrit:
ग्राह्यग्राहकसविवत्त् सामान्या सिधदेवहनाम् ।
योवगनां तु विशेषोऽवस्त सम्बन्धे सािधानता ॥ १०६ ॥
transliteration:
grāhya-grāhaka-saṃvittiḥ sāmānyā sarva-dehinām |
yogināṃ tu viśeṣo 'sti sambandhe sāvadhānatā || 106 ||
translation: The awareness consisting of the known and the knower is common to all embodied beings; but the distinction of yogins lies in careful attentiveness to their relation.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that yogic practice begins by closely observing the relationship between subject and object within experience.
beginner_explanation: Everyone experiences “I am seeing something” or “I am knowing something.” What makes a yogi different is not having special senses, but paying very close attention to this process itself. By watching how knower and known appear together, deeper insight opens.
scholar_explanation: Saṃvitti structured as grāhya and grāhaka is universal, but yogic viśeṣa arises through sāvadhānatā toward their sambandha. This points to reflexive awareness of cognition itself, where the apparent duality of subject-object can be examined and eventually resolved into nondual saṃvid. The verse is closely aligned with Pratyabhijñā analyses of pramātṛ-prameya relations as modalities of one consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Feeling Awareness in Another Body
sanskrit:
स्विदन्यशरीरेऽवऩ सविवत्तं अनुभाियेत् ।
अऩेऺां स्वशरीरस्य त्यक्त्वा व्याऩी वदनैर् भिेत् ॥ १०७ ॥
transliteration:
svadehād anya-śarīre 'pi saṃvittiṃ anubhāvayet |
apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī dinair bhavet || 107 ||
translation: One should experience awareness even in another's body; abandoning fixation on one's own body, one becomes all-pervading in the course of days.
intent_summary: The verse teaches expansion beyond self-centered embodiment by directly sensing consciousness as present in other bodies too.
beginner_explanation: Try to feel that the same aliveness that you know in yourself also lives in others. Let go of the habit of treating only your own body as “real me.” Over time, this practice can open a sense of shared being and spacious connection.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā extends saṃvitti beyond sva-śarīra into anya-śarīra, undermining the contracted individuality rooted in bodily exclusivity. The relinquishment of svaśarīrāpekṣā gradually yields vyāpti, an expansion into pervasive consciousness rather than empathetic imagination alone. In nondual Śaivism, the same cit-vimarśa shines through all bodies; the practice operationalizes that metaphysical claim contemplatively.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Mind Unsupported and Free of Conceptualization
sanskrit:
वनराधारं मन् कृत्वा विकल्पान्न विकल्पयेत् ।
तदात्मऩरमात्मत्वे भैरिो मृगऱोचने ॥ १०८ ॥
transliteration:
nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā vikalpān na vikalpayet |
tad-ātma-paramātmatve bhairavo mṛga-locane || 108 ||
translation: Making the mind unsupported, one should not fabricate conceptual constructions. Then, in the identity of self and Supreme Self, O doe-eyed one, there is Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse instructs the practitioner to let the mind rest without support and without conceptual proliferation, revealing the identity of individual and supreme consciousness.
beginner_explanation: Usually the mind holds onto something—a thought, memory, image, problem, or identity. Here the practice is to let it rest without leaning on anything at all. When that mental grasping stops, a deeper and more open sense of being can reveal itself.
scholar_explanation: Nirādhāra-manas is a key contemplative state in which mind is divested of object-support, and vikalpa is no longer reproduced by further vikalpa. In that cessation of conceptual superimposition, tad-ātma-paramātmatva—the identity of the limited self with Paramātman—is directly evident as Bhairava. This reflects the Trika movement from differentiated cognition into the uncontracted nondual saṃvid beyond pramāṇa structures.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Firm Recognition: I Am the All-Pervading Lord
sanskrit:
सिधऻ् सिधकताध च व्याऩक् ऩरमेश्वर् ।
स एिाहम् शैिधमाध इवत दार्ढ्ाधवच्छिो भिेत् ॥ १०९ ॥
transliteration:
sarvajñaḥ sarvakartā ca vyāpakaḥ parameśvaraḥ | 
sa evāhaṃ śaivadharmād iti dārḍhyāc chivo bhavet || 109 ||
translation: The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the doer of all, and all-pervading. “That very one am I, by the Śaiva dharma (or Śaiva teaching)”—through firmness in this, one becomes Śiva.
intent_summary: The verse teaches unwavering identification with the qualities of the Supreme Lord as a means of direct recognition of one's Śiva-nature.
beginner_explanation: This is a bold practice: instead of thinking of yourself as small and limited, reflect deeply that your true nature is the same vast consciousness called Śiva. Repeating this is not ego inflation; it is meant to dissolve the false small self. With steady conviction, identity shifts toward freedom.
scholar_explanation: The verse is explicitly pratyabhijñā-oriented: one recognizes oneself as the sarvajña, sarvakartṛ, vyāpaka Parameśvara. The phrase śaivadharmād may suggest grounding in the revealed Śaiva view or the intrinsic nature of consciousness disclosed thereby; dārḍhya is crucial, since unstable conceptual assent does not effect realization. This is not appropriation by ahaṃkāra but re-cognition of the true I-consciousness (pūrṇāham).

speaker: Bhairava
title: The Universe as Differentiated Rays of Bhairava
sanskrit:
जऱस्येिोमधयो िह्नेर्ज्ाधऱाभङ्ग्य् प्रभा रिे् ।
ममैि भैरिस्यैता विश्वभङ्ग्यो विभेवदता् ॥ ११० ॥
transliteration:
jalasyevormayo vahner jvālābhaṅgyāḥ prabhā raveḥ | 
mamaiva bhairavasya etā viśvabhaṅgyo vibheditāḥ || 110 ||
translation: As waves belong to water, as flickering tongues belong to fire, as rays belong to the sun—so these differentiated forms of the universe are of me alone, Bhairava.
intent_summary: The verse teaches that all differentiated phenomena are expressions of Bhairava, just as waves, flames, and rays are expressions of their source.
beginner_explanation: Waves are nothing but water in motion; sunlight rays are not separate from the sun. In the same way, all the many forms in the world are expressions of one reality. Seeing this helps dissolve the feeling that life is made of separate and disconnected things.
scholar_explanation: This verse gives classic emanational analogies: ūrmi-jala, jvālā-vahni, and prabhā-ravi. Difference (bheda, here vibhiditā or vibhinnatā implied in viśvabhaṅgyaḥ) is not denied, but understood as modal articulation of the one Bhairava. It therefore encapsulates nondual Śaiva cosmology: manifestation is real as self-expression (ābhāsa, śakti-vikāsa), yet never ontologically severed from its source.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Whirling Until the Shock Dissolves
sanskrit:
भ्रान्त्वा भ्रान्त्वा शरीरेण त्ववरतम् भुवि ऩातनात् ।
ऺोभशविविरामेण ऩरा संजायते दशा ॥ १११ ॥
transliteration: bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tvaritam bhuvi pātanāt | kṣobha-śakti-virāmeṇa parā sañjāyate daśā || 111 ||
translation: By spinning and whirling the body rapidly, then falling to the ground, when the agitating force (kṣobha-śakti) comes to rest, the supreme state arises.
intent_summary: Use intense bodily spinning followed by sudden collapse and stillness so that, in the cessation of inner agitation, a higher state reveals itself.
beginner_explanation: This practice uses strong motion to shake up your normal sense of balance and control. After spinning and dropping, there is a brief moment when the usual mental chatter can stop. The verse points to that pause after the disturbance, not the disturbance itself, as the doorway.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā works through induced kṣobha—an intentional perturbation of the psychophysical system—followed by its virāma, cessation. The point is not trance through exhaustion alone, but recognition of parā daśā in the interval after the collapse of kinetic and mental momentum. It parallels other VBT methods that exploit transitional gaps where vikalpa is stunned and awareness shines unobstructed.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Shock at the End of Energetic Penetration
sanskrit:
आधारेष्वथिाऽशक्त्याऽऻानावच्चत्तऱयेन िा ।
जातशविसमािेशऺोभान्ते भैरिं िऩु् ॥ ११२ ॥
transliteration: ādhāreṣv athavāśaktyā'jñānāvac-citta-layena vā | jāta-śakti-samāveśa-kṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuḥ || 112 ||
translation: Or, through penetration into the supports (ādhāras), through śakti, or through the mind's dissolution as if into not-knowing, at the end of the shock produced by the arising immersion in śakti (śakti-samāveśa), the form of Bhairava appears.
intent_summary: Enter deeply into subtle centers or energetic absorption, and at the end of the resulting inner upheaval, recognize the emergence of Bhairava.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes deep practice creates a strong inner surge, disorientation, or energy shift. This verse says that when that wave settles, something more fundamental can be noticed. Instead of fearing the change, the practitioner learns to notice the clear presence revealed after it.
scholar_explanation: The verse invokes ādhāras, śakti, and citta-laya, suggesting yogic absorption through subtle supports, energetic infusion, or suspension of ordinary mentation. The phrase ajñānāvat may indicate a state resembling blankness, yet the goal is not inert unconsciousness but the revelation of bhairavaṃ vapuḥ at the end of samāveśa-induced kṣobha. This is a classic Trika movement: śakti’s intensification culminates in recognition (pratyabhijñā) of Bhairava.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Still the Eyes to Enter Immediate Liberation
sanskrit:
सम्प्रदायवममं देवि शृणु सम्यविदाम्यहम् ।
कैिल्यं जायते सद्यो नेियो् स्तब्धमाियो् ॥ ११३ ॥
transliteration: sampradāyam imaṃ devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham | kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || 113 ||
translation: Hear this transmission (sampradāya), O Devī; I shall speak it rightly: liberation (kaivalya) arises immediately when the two eyes become simply still.
intent_summary: Steady the eyes completely and use that stillness as a direct means to immediate liberation.
beginner_explanation: When the eyes stop darting around, the mind often quiets too. This verse points to the simple act of letting the gaze become completely still. In that unmoving seeing, a deeper calm and freedom can appear.
scholar_explanation: The stilling of the dṛk-indriya here functions as an entry into kaivalya through arrest of ocular movement and the concomitant attenuation of vṛtti. Though expressed tersely, the verse aligns with tantric upāyas in which sensory fixation suspends discursivity and reveals the unmoving ground of awareness. The invocation of sampradāya suggests an esoteric practical instruction rather than a merely physiological observation.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Contract the Throat and Lower Gate
sanskrit:
सम्कोचं कणधयो् कृत्वा ह्यधोद्वारे तथैि च ।
अनच्कमहऱं ध्यायविशेद्ब्रह्म सनातनम् ॥ ११४ ॥
transliteration: saṃkocaṃ kaṇṭhayor kṛtvā hy adho-dvāre tathaiva ca | anaccha-mahalaṃ dhyāyan viśed brahma sanātanam || 114 ||
translation: Making contraction in the throat region, and likewise at the lower gate, meditating on the spotless great expanse, one enters the eternal Brahman.
intent_summary: Apply energetic locks above and below while contemplating the pure vastness, and thereby enter the eternal absolute.
beginner_explanation: This method combines body tension with meditation. By gently drawing in the throat and the lower pelvic area, attention becomes gathered and strong. While holding that collected feeling, one meditates on a clear, open vastness.
scholar_explanation: This appears to refer to bandha-like contractions at the kaṇṭha and adho-dvāra, likely analogous to jālandhara and mūla-related restraint. The bodily saṃkoca serves to contain and reverse the ordinary outward flow of prāṇa, while contemplation of the stainless vastness (anaccha-mahala) opens into brahma sanātanam. It exemplifies the VBT’s integration of somatic yoga and nondual contemplative recognition.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Gazing Down from a Great Height
sanskrit:
कूऩावदके महागते वस्थत्वोऩवर वनरीऺणात् ।
अविकल्पमते् सम्यक्सद्यवश्चत्तऱय् िुटम् ॥ ११५ ॥
transliteration: kūpādike mahā-garte sthitvopari nirīkṣaṇāt | avikalpa-mateḥ samyak sadyaś citta-layaḥ sphuṭam || 115 ||
translation: Standing above a well or other great abyss and gazing downward, for one whose mind becomes free of thought-constructs (avikalpa), there is at once a clear dissolution of mind.
intent_summary: Use the direct perception of depth and void to interrupt conceptual thought and induce dissolution of mind.
beginner_explanation: Looking into a deep drop can create a sudden, quiet alertness. For a moment, thoughts may stop because the mind is absorbed by the sheer openness. This verse uses that experience of depth as a doorway into inner stillness.
scholar_explanation: The visual confrontation with a mahā-garta functions as a support for avikalpa-mati, where the ordinary representational overlay is suspended. The resulting citta-laya is not merely fascination with danger but a collapse of discursivity before spatial vastness. As in other ākāśa-oriented dhāraṇās, external abyss mirrors the internal void of consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Wherever the Mind Goes, There Is Śiva
sanskrit:
यि यि मनो यावत िाह्ये िाभ्यन्तरेऽवऩ िा ।
ति ति वशिािास्था व्याऩकत्वात्क्व यास्यवत ॥ ११६ ॥
transliteration: yatra yatra mano yāti bāhye vābhyantare'pi vā | tatra tatra śivāvasthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati || 116 ||
translation: Wherever the mind goes—whether outward or inward—there, in each place, is the state of Śiva; because of all-pervasiveness, where could it go?
intent_summary: Recognize that every movement of mind occurs only within the all-pervasive state of Śiva.
beginner_explanation: Usually we think some thoughts are spiritual and others are distractions. This verse says that whatever appears in the mind, inside or outside, happens within one vast presence. Instead of fighting experience, notice the space in which all experience occurs.
scholar_explanation: This is a direct nondual instruction grounded in Śiva’s vyāpakatva, all-pervasiveness. The verse undermines the inward/outward dichotomy and reframes mental movement itself as never departing from śivāvasthā. It resonates strongly with Pratyabhijñā doctrine: there is no locus outside consciousness for the mind to travel to.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Trace Every Cognition to Consciousness
sanskrit:
यि यिाऺमागेण चैतन्यं व्यज्यते विभो् ।
तस्य तन्मािधवमधत्वावच्चल्लयाद्भवरतात्मता ॥ ११७ ॥
transliteration: yatra yatrākṣa-mārgeṇa caitanyaṃ vyajyate vibhoḥ | tasya tan-mātra-dharmitvāc chillayād bharitātmatā || 117 ||
translation: Wherever, through the path of the senses, the consciousness of the All-pervading One becomes manifest, because that object has the nature of that alone, by dissolving into consciousness (cit-laya) one attains fullness of Self.
intent_summary: In every sensory experience, recognize consciousness itself shining there, and dissolve attention into that to realize fullness.
beginner_explanation: Every sight, sound, or touch is not just an object—it is also an experience lit up by awareness. This verse says to notice that aware quality instead of getting lost in the object. When you do, experience feels fuller and less separate.
scholar_explanation: The sensory channels (akṣa-mārga) are not obstacles but loci where vibhu-caitanya becomes explicit. Since the object is of the nature of ‘that alone’ (tan-mātra-dharmitvāt), one can shift from object-fixation to cit-laya, dissolving into the conscious luminosity underlying appearance. Bharitātmatā here suggests plenary selfhood, akin to the pūrṇatā of Bhairava-consciousness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: At the End of Hunger, Fear, or Shock
sanskrit:
ऺुताद्यन्ते भये शोके गह्वरे िा रणाद्द्रुते ।
कुतूहऱेऺुधाद्यन्ते ब्रह्मसत्तामयी दशा ॥ ११८ ॥
transliteration: kṣutādyante bhaye śoke gahvare vā raṇād drute | kutūhalekṣudhādyante brahma-sattā-mayī daśā || 118 ||
translation: At the end of hunger and such states, in fear, in grief, in a chasm, when fleeing from battle, in intense curiosity, and at the end of craving and the like—there is a state filled with the reality of Brahman.
intent_summary: Notice the raw, exposed state present at the peak or ending of intense human experiences, where the reality of Brahman can become evident.
beginner_explanation: Strong experiences—fear, grief, hunger, urgency, intense curiosity—can strip away our usual mental routines. In those moments, there can be a naked, vivid presence underneath the emotion. This verse says that if you notice carefully, that bare presence is spiritually significant.
scholar_explanation: This dhāraṇā exploits liminal psychophysical intensities where habitual conceptual structuring is interrupted. The phrase brahma-sattā-mayī daśā indicates that the practitioner should detect the ontological immediacy shining in such extremities, not merely the affective content itself. It stands alongside other VBT methods that leverage thresholds, shocks, and the exhaustion of drive to reveal the non-conceptual ground.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Abandon the Mind in Remembered or Seen Objects
sanskrit:
िस्तुषु स्मयधमाणेषु दृष्टे देशे मनस् त्यजेत् ।
स्वशरीरं वनराधारं कृत्वा प्रसरवत प्रभु् ॥ ११९ ॥
transliteration: vastuṣu smaryamāṇeṣu dṛṣṭe deśe manas tyajet | sva-śarīraṃ nirādhāraṃ kṛtvā prasarati prabhuḥ || 119 ||
translation: When objects are being remembered, or in a place being seen, one should abandon the mind there; making one's own body unsupported, the Lord (prabhuḥ) expands.
intent_summary: Let go of mental fixation on remembered or presently seen objects, and release bodily support so that expansive consciousness can unfold.
beginner_explanation: When you remember something or look at something, the mind usually grabs onto it. This verse says: stop holding it mentally. If you also relax the felt sense of your body being tightly fixed and solid, awareness can open out more widely.
scholar_explanation: To ‘abandon the mind’ in relation to remembered or perceived objects means relinquishing appropriation and conceptual support at the point of cognition. The instruction to render the body nirādhāra suggests loosening embodied localization, allowing prabhu—expansive consciousness—to prasarati, unfold or extend. This is a subtle transition from object-directed cognition to unsupported awareness.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Fix the Gaze on an Object Until Emptiness Opens
sanskrit:
क्ववचद्वस्तुवन विन्यस्य शनैदृधवष्टम् वनितधयेत् ।
तज्ज्ञानं वचत्तसवहतं देवि शून्याऱायो भिेत् ॥१२० ॥
transliteration: kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanair dṛṣṭiṃ nivartayet | taj jñānaṃ citta-sahitaṃ devi śūnyālayaḥ bhavet || 120 ||
translation: Placing the gaze upon some object, then slowly withdrawing it, that knowledge together with the mind, O Devī, becomes established in the abode of emptiness (śūnyālaya).
intent_summary: Use steady looking and gradual withdrawal of the gaze to let cognition and mind sink into emptiness.
beginner_explanation: First, look steadily at a single object. Then slowly ease the gaze back or inward without abruptly breaking attention. The verse says this can draw the mind away from ordinary fixation and into a spacious inner emptiness.
scholar_explanation: This resembles a subtle form of dṛṣṭi-yoga or proto-trāṭaka, but the crucial movement is nivartana—the gradual withdrawal of sight from objectification. When object-knowledge (taj jñānam) and citta are recollected from dispersion, they settle into śūnyālaya, the locus of emptiness. The technique thus moves from visual support to non-conceptual spatial absorption.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Śāṅkarī State Through Surge of Devotion
sanskrit:
भक्त्युद्रेकावद्वरिस्य यादृशी जायते मवत् ।
सा शवि् शाङ्करी वनत्यं भियेत्तां तत् वशि् ॥ १२१ ॥
transliteration:
bhaktyudrekād viraktasya yādṛśī jāyate matiḥ |
sa śaktiḥ śāṅkarī nityaṃ bhāvayet tāṃ tataḥ vaśī || 121 ||
translation: When, through an upsurge of devotion (bhakti), there arises in the detached one a particular state of mind, that is the Śāṅkarī Śakti. One should continually contemplate that; then one becomes self-mastered (vaśī).
intent_summary: Recognize the elevated inner state born of intense devotion and stabilize attention in it until it becomes an abiding power.
beginner_explanation: Sometimes deep devotion or love for the divine creates a clear, uplifted inner feeling. This verse says: do not let that moment pass unnoticed. Stay with that sacred feeling and let it steady your whole being.
scholar_explanation: The verse identifies the bhaktyudreka-generated matiḥ as Śāṅkarī Śakti, the power of Śaṅkara manifest in affective consciousness. This is not mere emotionalism, but a refined devotional cognition in a virakta practitioner, capable of becoming a dhāraṇā. Sustained bhāvana of this śakti yields vaśitva, mastery or integration of the psychospiritual field.

speaker: Bhairava
title: Meditation on the Void Between States
sanskrit:
िस्त्वन्तरे िेद्यमाने सिधिस्तुषु शून्यता ।
तामेि मनसा ध्यात्वा विवदतोऽवऩ प्रशाम्यवत ॥ १२२ ॥
transliteration:
sarvasv-antara-vedyamāne siddhis tuṣu śūnyatā |
tām eva manasā dhyātvā nirvikalpo'vaśāmyati || 122 ||
